title: Opinion: Countesswells Development Limited v Scottish Hydro Electric Transmission plc
text:
Lands Tribunal for Scotland

OPINION

Countesswells Development Limited (Applicants) v Scottish Hydro Electric Transmission plc (Respondents)

Application for Determination of Question of Disputed Compensation Countesswells, Aberdeen

Introduction

[1] This case is an application for determination of a question of disputed compensation. The applicants claim compensation under paragraph 7(1) of Schedule 4 to the Electricity Act 1989 (“the 1989 Act”). Scottish Ministers have granted necessary wayleaves in favour of the respondents for a period of 50 years through land belonging to the applicants. The wayleaves relate to an overhead transmission line (“the OHL”) at Countesswells, Aberdeen. The applicants own and control a large portion of a development site there. The applicants firstly claim loss of development value of £10.75m in a transmission line corridor in respect that dwellings cannot be built there. The value is described in more detail in the pleadings as hope value. The applicants secondly seek compensation in the sum of approximately £2.7m in name of injurious affection. It is contended that there will be a diminution in value of dwellings to be constructed along a 25m corridor on either side of the no build corridor.

[2] More specifically the applicants have produced a plan (“Plan 2,” JB2, Appendix A to this Opinion) showing an area of land in their ownership comprising a 40m wide inner transmission line corridor. This is a no build zone. It extends to 3.1302ha. There are adjacent areas (“nibs”) where development has also been prevented for design reasons on account of the no build zone, but where there would otherwise have been potential for development. These areas extend to a further 1.2545ha, thus resulting in a contended total loss of building land amounting to 4.39ha (10.85 acres). The applicants have produced a table calculating that without the OHL an additional 138 units could have been constructed on development blocks N2, N13, N4, C6 and C7. The table assumes the additional units would be built at the same density as the “with scheme” units in the respective proposed blocks. Not all of N2 belongs to the applicants and the relevant portion is not included in the above measurements, so the claim has been based on a loss of 128 units. For the purposes of the injurious affection claim, Plan 2 also shows the outer transmission corridor extending 25m in width on either side of the 40m wide inner corridor. The outer corridor therefore lies between 20m and 45m on either side of the centre line of the inner corridor. The outer corridor extends to 2.922ha (7.22 acres). It is contended that dwellings built within this corridor will be diminished in value on account of the OHL.

Procedure

[3] The respondents recovered various documents under specification relating to comparable land sales and option agreements. The applicants claimed confidentiality on the basis that these documents were commercially sensitive. We allowed the documents to be recovered on the basis of confidentiality undertakings being provided by relevant members of the respondents’ team. This Opinion will seek to avoid going into detail about these transactions except where consistent with providing adequate reasoning for our findings.

[4] We held an accompanied site visit on 29 October 2020. There was an unaccompanied part of the visit which included neighbouring areas and various off-site comparators. There was a further unaccompanied visit on 30 September 2021. At our request parties provided an agreed analysis of comparable transactions in the form of a table (JB117). Parties also provided a Scott Schedule (JB 118) for their respective inputs for a residual appraisal valuation for the “lost” areas of development land. The Scott Schedule is Appendix B to this Opinion. The table and schedule were prepared by Mr Court and Mr Stevens. We have slightly altered the main heading of the Scott Schedule consistent with the fact that a number of the boxes are potentially applicable to both residual appraisals and comparative valuations. The boxes applicable to both methods are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10 and 14. The boxes generally applicable only to the residual method are boxes 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 and 22. Box 21 is only applicable to the comparative method. We have provided our own entries for a number of the boxes as reflected in this Opinion.

[5] The full hearing was delayed for covid related reasons. The hearing took place on 2, 3, 9, 10, 13-17, 27 and 28 September with closing submissions on 13-14 October 2021. The hearing proceeded both remotely and in person. This was the first “lengthy” Tribunal case to proceed mainly in person under covid restrictions. We would express our appreciation to all participants for their professionalism and, at times, their forbearance in this matter.

[6] The applicants called six witnesses. They were Stephen Loomes, Richard Fawcus and James Fitzsimons who at relevant times were employed by the Stuart Milne Group Ltd (“SMG”). Mr Loomes is a chartered town planner and was managing director of SMG’s strategic land division. Mr Fawcus is a member of the RICS and is employed by SMG as a land and commercial director. Prior to his retirement Mr Fitzsimons was also a member of the RICS and was employed as the Countesswells project director and subsequently as a special projects director. The applicants also called expert witnesses, namely, Mr Pol MacDonald, Mr John Findlay and Mr Michael Court. Mr MacDonald is a landscape architect and founding director of OPEN with experience in large scale masterplanning. Mr Findlay is a chartered town planner, member of the RTPI and consultant with Ryden LLP with significant experience in the Aberdeen area. Mr Court is a member of the RICS and partner in DM Hall LLP , with experience in the valuation of development land. The applicants were represented by Mr James Findlay QC .

[7] The respondents led the evidence of nine witnesses namely George Leggat, Iain Richmond, Niall McLeod, Ewan Thomson, Daniel Lewis, James Truscott, Steven Black, Eric Shearer and Eric Stevens. Mr Leggat is a member of the RICS and is head of land assembly for the respondents. Mr Richmond is an employee of SHEPD and member of their wayleave policy team. Mr McLeod at the relevant time was a land director in Aberdeen for house builders Dandara Limited. Mr Thomson is a solicitor with CMS Cameron McKenna Nabarro Olswang LLP based in Edinburgh. His evidence was agreed. Mr Lewis is the development management manager at Aberdeen City Council (“ACC”) and amongst other things is responsible for the Council’s masterplanning, design and conservation (“MDC”) team. Mr Truscott is a landscape architect and consultant with Ash Design + Assessment Limited (“ASH”), chartered landscape architects. Mr Black is a member of the RTPI and lead director of the Scottish Planning and Development Team at Jones Lang LaSalle (“JLL”) based in Edinburgh. Mr Shearer is managing partner at Knight Frank LLP based in Aberdeen. He is a member of the RICS with expertise in the property development sector. Mr Stevens is a director at JLL and member of the RICS with experience in commercial valuation and evaluation of residential land. The respondents were represented by Ms Ailsa Wilson QC and Mr Graham Middleton, advocate.

[8] The planning profession generally specifies measurements in metric with area in hectares (ha) and sqm. The property industry generally specifies area in imperial measurement, i.e. in square feet and acres. This Opinion generally follows this dual approach as context requires.

[9] We allowed productions JB 126-134 to be lodged by the respondents at a late stage in the proceedings. The documents relate to an “updated” injurious affection study at the Dandara Hazelwood site. The applicants did not object to it, but subject to the caveat, to which we agreed, that the applicants’ witnesses have not been able to comment upon it.

[10] We received extensive written closing submissions which had been prepared in the period following conclusion of the evidence. Oral submissions were made in response. After we made avizandum we received a request from the respondents the following week seeking to be allowed to make a further written submission. They explained that senior counsel had not been fully fit at the time of the oral submissions and had overlooked a specific matter on which she wished to respond. We were informed that the matter had been covered in the respondents’ written submission but it was sought to be expanded upon. The point in question was not specified in the request. The request was opposed by the applicants. We declined the request on the basis that we were unable to identify any critical gap in the submissions as to justify a significant departure from normal procedure.

[11] During our deliberations we discovered an error in certain area calculations. We drew this to parties’ attention on 2 November 2021. After various correspondence, culminating on 21 January 2022, parties agreed the extent of the recalculated areas, which we shall adopt in this Opinion.

[12] We were advised that the applicants went into administration on 23 rd November 2021. We were advised that the Administrators instructed the claim to continue.

Legislation

Electricity Act 1989 (Schedule 4 paragraph 7(1))

Paragraph 7 provides:

“7(1) where a wayleave is granted to a licence holder under paragraph 6 above-

(a) The occupier of the land; and

(b) Where the occupier is not also the owner of the land, the owner,

may recover from the licence holder compensation in respect of the grant.”

Glossary

ACC:
Aberdeen City Council, the planning authority.
ASH:
the respondents’ landscape architects.
CAAD:
Certificate of appropriate alternative development.
CDL:
the applicants Countesswells Development Ltd.
CDFMP:
Countesswells Development Framework and Masterplan, prepared by OPEN. This Opinion uses it as is a general expression covering the Countesswells Development Framework and Phase 1 Masterplan adopted as SG by ACC in 2014; and the Phase 1B Masterplan adopted as an Addendum to the SG by ACC in 2017.
dpa:
dwellings per acre
ES:
Environmental Statement prepared circa 2014, submitted in support of the application for PPiP.
Headline Price:
the price of development land calculated for comparative purposes. Involves adding to the net price paid the cost of any agreements under section 75 of the 1997 Act and the cost of any abnormal site works. Also known as the greenfield price.
LDP:
Aberdeen Local Development Plan 2017, superseded the 2012 LDP.
LVIA:
Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment.
MDC:
Masterplanning, Design and Conservation team at ACC’s planning department.
MSC:
Application for Matters Specified in Conditions under a PPiP under regulation 12 of the 2013 Regulations.
N2 Developer Brief:
A developer brief issued by CDL to planning officers in 2018 for discussion purposes. It included a section known as Option 1b identifying an expansion area for additional housing for block N2 based on a scenario that the OHL was removed.
Necessary Wayleaves:
the statutory wayleaves granted by Scottish Ministers on 1 August 2018 under Schedule 4 of the Electricity Act 1989. These are WAY-100-6 affecting the northern OHL corridor and WAY-100-17 affecting the southern OHL corridor.
Net Density:
housing density provided under planning policies, calculations for a net site area being the gross site area less deductions for areas of community facilities, open space and strategic roads.
NDA:
Net Developable Acreage, calculated in a similar way to net site area above.
OHL:
The existing 132kV overhead transmission line.
OHL Corridor:
a 40m wide no build zone extending from a centre line 20m on either side of the pylons. Also described as the inner corridor. There is a north and south corridor in the applicants’ ownership, intersected by a block of forestry outwith the applicants’ ownership. In context as used in this Opinion, the term may include the additional areas hatched red on plan 2 (the “nibs”).
OHL Outer Corridor:
A further 25m strip extending either side of the inner corridor upon which the applicants have based an injurious affection claim.
OPEN:
Optimised Environments Ltd, a multi-disciplinary design company appointed by SMG/CDL to undertake masterplanning for a new settlement at Countesswells.
PPiP:
Planning Permission in Principle, defined under paragraph 3 of the 2013 Regulations.
The PPiP:
The Planning Permission in Principle for a residential led mixed use development of approximately 3000 homes at Countesswells. ACC determined a “willingness to approve” on 8 October 2014, and issued a consent on 1 April 2016 following conclusion of a legal agreement.
Relevant Date:
1 August 2018.
RSL:
Registered Social Landlord.
RVAA:
Residential Visual Amenity Assessment.
SDP:
Strategic Development Plan, approved by Scottish Ministers in 2014, replaced 2009 Structure Plan.
SG:
Supplementary Guidance, defined under section 22 of the 1997 Act.
SHEPD:
Scottish Hydro Electric Power Distribution Ltd, deals with transmission of electricity up to 33kV.
SHETL:
the respondents, Scottish Hydro Electric Transmission Plc.
SMG:
Stewart Milne Group Ltd.
SPP:
Scottish Planning Policy.

Background facts and circumstances

The site

[13] There are eight very large housing developments taking place in and around Aberdeen. One of these is at Countesswells. Countesswells lies about four miles west from the city centre. The LDP boundary area is 165.9ha or 410 acres. It is irregularly shaped but at its longest is well over a mile from north to south and at its widest is nearly one mile across from east to west. It is designated site OP38 in the 2017 LDP where it has an allocation of 3,000 homes and 10ha of employment land.

[14] The site is traditional farmland. It is contained within a natural bowl in the landscape, rising from south to north. To the east lies Hazlehead Woods and beyond that Hazlehead Park, which contains golf courses, tennis courts, sports pitches and horse riding facilities. To the west lies Countesswells Woods. To the south lies Foggieton Woods. The north has a more open aspect. Overall the site is well contained and not readily visible from other settlements.

Planning history

[15] The 2009 structure plan allocated new 36,000 houses to Aberdeen City for the period to 2030, with a large number of them proposed for greenfield sites. There was a bid process in 2009 for the purpose of identifying sites for allocation in the proposed LDP. There was also a greenbelt review looking to the preferred sites to determine whether a site’s suitability for development outweighed its suitability in meeting greenbelt objectives. This led to the allocation of 3,000 houses at Countesswells under designation OP58 in the 2012 LDP, and 10ha of employment land. According to the report of the examination in public ACC’s calculation of numbers was based upon a net density of 30 dwellings per hectare. This was a rough calculation based upon a gross density of 20 dwellings per hectare x 155.18 ha = 3,102 rounded to 3,000. The allocation was carried forward to the current LDP to provide 2,150 homes to 2016 and 850 homes to 2026.

[16] The lead developer assembling the site was SMG. OPEN began designing the site for development in 2012. A full environmental impact assessment was required, which took the form of an ES dated March 2014. Under the LDP the site required masterplanning. OPEN prepared the Countesswells Development Framework and Masterplan for various phases “the CDFMP.” The CDFMP itself envisaged that it would become adopted SG by ACC and thus form part of the statutory development plan. The development framework and phase 1 of the masterplan was duly adopted by ACC as SG during 2014, and forwarded to Scottish Ministers for ratification. The document sets out in some detail applicable design principles by means of text and detailed plans. An application for PPiP for a mixed use development of approximately 3,000 houses and others was made in 2014, considered by the full council and approved subject to the conclusion of a section 75 agreement. The PPiP application thus coincided with the adoption of the CDFMP. The permission was granted on 1 April 2016 following conclusion of the agreement. The main text of the permission letter expressly refers to the application form and docqueted documents and plans which comprised two plans, namely a site location plan and a boundary plan. The conditions refer to other matters which we shall refer to later.

[17] The CDFMP was amended by means of an addendum in 2017. This modified the development framework and set out a phase 1B masterplan. The addendum took account of various design changes, including a realigned access road and a smaller primary school site. There were detailed changes to the phasing strategy and a revised indicative number of housing units to 3,090, i.e. an increase of 90 units due to the reduction in the school area. Development blocks affected by the northern OHL corridor, namely N2, N13 and N4 were included in phase 1b of the project. Two blocks affected by the southern portion of the OHL corridor, namely blocks C6 and C7, were already included in the discussion and plans of design principles in the original document. The addendum moved blocks C6 and C7 and certain others from phase 1 to phase 2 of the project, i.e. to a later stage than N2, N13 and N4 and others. ACC agreed to adopt the CDFMP addendum as SG on 15 March 2017 following a period of public consultation, which was sent to Scottish Ministers for ratification.

The OHL

[18] There are three 132 kV OHLs which transverse the site. One crosses a westmost area, and another crosses the southern tip. The third OHL which is in issue here runs between Kintore and Craigiebuckler. It has existed for many years. It crosses the eastern portion of the site in an approximate south-east/north-west line. The OHL is in effect separated into a north and south corridor whereby the sections are divided by a block of forestry. This forestry block is outwith the LDP allocation boundary and is not, as we understood it, within the control of the applicants, although it does lie within the PPiP red line boundary.

[19] There are six pylons numbered 50-55 running through the development corridor for about three quarters of a mile. For present purposes pylons 50 and 51 lie adjacent to blocks N2, N3 and N13, and pylons 53 and 54 lie adjacent to blocks C6 and C7. Pylon 50 lies outwith the part of N2 owned by CDL. Pylon 52 lies within the block of forestry and no. 55 lies outwith the area for which compensation is claimed. The pylons are 29m high. They have six arms carrying a total of six conductors, and an earth wire running from the top of the pylons. They are by no means the largest pylons operated by the respondents, who operate 275 kV and 400 kV transmission lines elsewhere. Without going into detail, the 40m wide no build corridor is based upon technical health and safety guidance for OHL operators, and upon construction regulations for housebuilders. The corridor also prevents trees being grown above a certain height.

[20] The respondents’ right to keep the OHL on the land was, at its highest, based upon a longstanding personal wayleave agreement with previous landowners. It would appear that SMG/CDL had not initially realised that they were entitled to seek removal of the OHL without cost to themselves. Mr MacDonald of OPEN explained that he commenced designing the development site in 2012 assuming the OHL would remain in situ . However, at some point in 2016 the applicants realised they could serve notices requiring removal of the OHL. Notices were served on 1 December 2016. The respondents duly lodged applications for statutory wayleaves under the 1989 Act. A hearing was held by an inquiry reporter in February 2018. The applicants made written representations but did not appear in person. Amongst other things the reporter considered an options report for possible rerouting and/or undergrounding the OHL. Her report made recommendations dated 12 July 2018. She considered that it was both necessary and expedient that the relevant apparatus remain in its current position and recommended that the applications be granted for a 50 year duration. Scottish Ministers agreed with the reporter’s recommendations and granted the necessary wayleaves on 1 August 2018. This is the relevant date for compensation purposes.

Site assembly and development

[21] The site involved several landholdings of some complexity. It comprises various portions of land known as Bellfield Farm, Boatwynd, Loanhead Farm, Wardhead Farm, Mains of Countesswells and Colthill Farm. Much of the land was acquired by SMG and associates over a period of years. As part of a business transfer agreement of March 2016, CDL acquired the Countesswells assets including the land. This was necessary to enable CDL to participate in a UK government infrastructure guarantee scheme, in effect guaranteeing loans for provision of infrastructure. As at the relevant date, CDL owned most of the north of the development site excluding certain northmost and westmost portions. They also held options to the southern part of the site comprising Mains of Countesswells and Colthill. A Mains of Countesswells option agreement was triggered during 2018. As at the relevant date, it is estimated that CDL controlled approximately 80% of the CDFMP area, including those areas subject to option agreements.

[22] As can be seen from Plan 2 the site was divided into “N” “C” and “S” (north, central and south) development blocks. In general terms CDL undertook responsibility for the main infrastructure works for the project. This work commenced on site in 2016. We understood that SMG constructed most or all of the affordable homes on site themselves, on behalf of registered social landlords (“RSLs”). The land for private homes was either developed by SMG or sold on to other private developers. SMG commenced construction of private and affordable homes on block N10 in 2016. Construction commenced on further affordable homes in 2017 on block C4. Block C2 was sold to Kirkwood Homes in January 2018, block N6 was sold to Barratt Homes in May 2018 and part of block C3 was sold to CHAP in August 2018, all for private housing. These housebuilders commenced construction during 2018. By August 2018, 150 homes had been completed and inhabited. Development was contained in relatively central parts of the site at this stage. In August 2019 CDL sold further land at N12, N5 and C3 to Hillcrest Homes for affordable housing. In February 2020, CDL sold a large tranche of land to BDW Trading Ltd (in effect Barratt Homes) for the construction of 468 private units. This sale related to blocks C1, N2, N3, N4 and N13 and included areas of the pylon land. There was also an excambion which we need not detail here.

Open space, the OHL and the CDFMP

[23] The CDFMP provides (p54 et seq ) for areas of open space throughout the development. The most significant of these are the Cults Burn Corridor network (11.02ha) and Countesswells Central Park (2.6ha). There is a good number of other open space areas. The document treats the OHL no build corridor as open space. The landscape strategy shows the northern OHL corridor as Hazleden Park, initially to comprise 2ha of land. Hazleden Park includes a large play area and allotments. (It should not be confused with the existing nearby Hazlehead Park outwith the site). The addendum indicates detailed design principles for Hazleden Park (p168). These also include path connections, informal spaces to the north and a more formal park design to the south.

[24] The CDFMP shows the open space of the OHL southern corridor in two sections. There is an area of general open space of a somewhat irregular nature. Some witnesses described this as the “central” area of OHL open space corridor, or “area 9”. This area had initially been calculated by Mr Stevens at 1.29ha (3.19 acres). Further south there is Wardhead Park consisting of 1.1ha including a play zone.

[25] The areas for Hazleden Park, the central area and Wardhead Park have been recalculated after the hearing, following the identification of an arithmetical error. The error did not relate to the areas specified in Appendix A (Plan 2), but to how the areas are apportioned among the three areas of open space. We also were told that Hazleden Park had been reduced in size by the 2017 addendum from 2 ha to 1.76 ha. This reduction would appear to be implied by certain drawings in the addendum. Part of the area (0.34 ha) of the proposed park belongs to a third party, leaving the applicants with 1.42 ha of Hazleden Park. Wardhead Park has been more accurately measured at 1.15 ha, not 1.1 ha stated in the CDFMP. The central area has been recalculated at 1.82 ha, not 1.29 ha referred to by Mr Stevens, which area includes the no build zone and the nibs. The total no build area including the nibs remains at 4.39 ha.

[26] Hazleden Park and Wardhead Park are described as local open space. Hazleden Park is also described as providing an outdoor sports area. Wardhead Park and the central area are described as providing natural green space and green corridors. In the 2014 CDFMP Hazleden Park is described as contributing to a requirement for outdoor sports areas. The 2017 Addendum (p169) refers to there being no formal requirement for sports pitches within the park space, but that the southern part of Hazleden Park would provide a location for the large play zone and a variety of informal sports areas.

N2 Developer Brief

[27] In autumn 2018 the applicants commenced discussions with ACC planning officers concerning an “N2 Developer Brief.” The applicants were intending to go to market on block N2 in the north of the site and wished to obtain officers’ views on design issues set out in the document. Thus prospective purchasing developers would have a clearer idea as to what proposals would be more likely to find favour with officials. It was essentially an evolution of the phase 1b masterplan addendum specifically for the N2 area. However the document also included a few pages referring to a “potential N2 expansion area”. The document referred to a scenario in which the pylons and overhead lines were removed and proposed an option for utilising previously “sterilised” land for the logical expansion of N2 eastwards. The document stated: “The open space created by the “no build” zone is not a requirement of the Development Framework or Masterplan in terms of design or meeting placemaking aspirations.” The brief included various text and plans showing how an expanded N2 area over the OHL no build corridor could add 15 units to the development block. A number of “key design principles” relating to the expanded block N2 area were specified. The document shows an intent to redesign the adjoining area N13, also affected by the OHL corridor, to include a large play area in substitution for the large play area lost by the removal of Hazleden Park.

[28] The applicants provided supporting information, (also referred to as “Option 1b.”) This information included a “Plan 3” showing that with the OHL removed, and reflecting the density and design aspirations for surrounding parcels, an additional 138 units could be delivered on the north and south portions of the no build corridor. Plan 3 indicated that were the OHL to be removed, and the OHL corridor to be used for housing, ACC’s guidance would require 20.53ha of open space for a total of 3,228 homes (i.e. 3,000 + 90 + 138). There would remain open space provision of 27.98ha across the site, well in excess of ACC’s requirements and consistent with the development framework’s principles on open space. The supporting information also included the table indicating upon which blocks the additional units might go, at a similar density to the block densities provided under the CDFMP.

[29] The discussions were led for the applicants by Mr Macdonald from a technical perspective, and involved Mr Fitzsimons from a client’s perspective. The discussions involved ACC’s MDC team which had been involved in the evolution of the CDFMP. The discussions involved Mr Sandy Beattie, MDC team leader, and subsequently by Ms Claire McArthur, who became MDC team leader. Other members of ACC’s team included Rebecca Kerr, a masterplanner and Dineke Brasier, a senior planner and development manager. The discussions were by telephone and email as well as at least two meetings.

[30] The discussions produced two formal letters from ACC’s MDC team, on the headed notepaper for ACC’s department of Strategic Place Planning. The first was from Mr Beattie to Mr Fitzsimons dated 14 December 2018. We shall quote most of this letter in full:-

“Countesswells Development Area N2 Options

You presented an alternative proposal for the N2 area of Countesswells which indicated an alternative layout for the area should the existing pylon line be rerouted or undergrounded.

As the development framework and masterplan stand, the area currently assigned to the overhead electricity lines results in a restrictive land use which is not complimentary to the high residential quality of place intended at Countesswells. Although designated as open space in the framework, it is restrictive in use and does not sit well with surrounding residential and education uses along the eastern edges of Countesswells.

I am mindful of the quality placemaking outcomes that both Countesswells Development Limited and Aberdeen City Council have been striving to achieve in Countesswells – the overhead electricity supply running through the site is a barrier to achieving that.

Your alternative development proposal, as identified in drawing … plan 3 Potential Layout …, indicates the potential site capacity should the overhead lines be removed. This would, in my view, present a far more welcome approach to placemaking, health and wellbeing and indeed improved perception of Countessswells as a desirable mixed community to live in.

I agree in principle that there is potential for an increase in the number of housing units, which will require to be robustly tested against planning policy and the ambitions set out in the development framework. Your table indicates a provisional uplift in the number of housing units based on the additional land becoming available. It should also be noted that open space contributions will require to be considered as part of that scenario. You will be aware that we generally seek quality of space, clearly defined, rather than quantity, which will be far more desirable than is currently proposed under an overhead line. Again, this can be tested against planning policy.

In short, I would welcome further discussion on the potential to provide additional units in the N2 area, should the pylons be removed. Should the overhead line be removed, I believe that there is capacity to increase the number of units, review density and deliver significant improvements to the quality of place, open space and placemaking ambition in this development area. The specific number will be achieved by a detailed review of the framework capacity, which we will be happy to work with you on. …”.

[31] On 10 January 2019, Mr Beattie emailed Mr Macdonald as follows:-

“As you know we are very much in favour of the principle of a developer brief for all development areas of Countesswells. The draft brief is a positive start and I think there are a few issues particularly pertinent to N2 that would benefit from further detail and refinement.

We are certainly in favour of the pylons line being removed. It should be absolutely clear that the open space removed as a result is either compensated for elsewhere or is surplus to policy requirements. The open space around the pylons also served to provide a clear landscape break between character areas N2 and N3, so it is important to understand how that is handled to avoid an amorphous mass of housing.

An issue raised previously is the strong line of housing along the northern boundary and how a more naturalised and positive landscape edge could be achieved. Again, this was something that the landscape break for the pylons helped to address. I would be looking to make that edge much more irregular and less formal …”

[32] A final version of the N2 brief was forwarded to ACC on 22 March 2019. At this point Mr Macdonald asked ACC for their position, hitherto stated by email, to be stated on a simple ACC letter format which could be issued to future developers. This resulted in the second formal letter from ACC to Mr Fitzsimons. Mr Beattie had moved on to a new role as Queen Street Masterplan Manager. Mr Lewis indicated that the correspondence in question was of a nature which he would expect the MDC team to have discussed with developers. [82] Mr Lewis stated that he had not seen the N2 Developer Brief when he gave his written statement in October 2020. However, after he gave evidence he appears to have reflected on the matter. The respondents subsequently produced an affidavit in which he states that he had in fact received the developer brief in July 2020. We allowed the affidavit to be received.

[83] He interpreted the ACC letters as providing a planning officer’s initial view to give developers guidance for further development at Countesswells. The correspondence related to a routine planning query, namely changes in the layout of a large scheme. He had not been aware of the letters and background at the time, and accepted he was less familiar with the issues than those dealing with the correspondence.

[84] The PPiP applied to the whole red bound line boundary of the site. He thought internal zones or blocks could be adjusted by subsequent variations to the masterplan or by subsequent MSC applications. An MSC application would not necessarily be reported to committee. That would only occur if triggered under delegated powers procedures such as by receiving more than six objections, or objections by a statutory consultee or a community council. If an MSC application came in seeking housing on the OHL land on N2, as a matter of competency ACC would deal with it under the PPiP. If the CDFMP were to be formally amended, he did not think that Scottish Ministers would likely get involved for the sake of 120 additional houses. On the other hand he thought that if, for example, proposals involved the loss of the Cults Burn corridor, he would expect ministers to get involved. The Cults Burn corridor was a key feature. He did not consider the OHL corridor to be a key feature since the corridor only existed because the OHL was there. It was not a key link under the masterplan.

[85] The PPiP allowed for a certain amount of flexibility by variations to the masterplan or through MSC applications. It would be a judgement call whether a proposal would require to be dealt with by a new planning application, an MSC application or as a non-material variation. Depending upon the scale of the proposal the development framework might need to be reviewed.

[86] Mr Lewis considered that for a full planning decision to be made on the N2 brief and the OHL corridor, more detail would be required. As Mr Beattie’s letter said, the proposal would require to be tested against planning policy and the ambitions set out in the development framework. It was not a foregone conclusion that planning permission would have been granted.

[87] As an initial view he did not think it likely that a change involving removal of the OHL corridor for houses would trigger the requirement for a further EIA. The site did not contain significant wildlife or have a high ecological value, and the impact was site specific. The ES commitments showed what should be done at the site generally and was not zone specific. Absent detailed information however he could not categorically confirm that a further EIA would not be required. He felt it unlikely that SNH/NatureScot would get involved since they only wished to be consulted if there were high value wildlife issues. Objections from the public would be less likely prior to the relevant date simply because there were fewer residents at Countesswells than after that date.

[88] If an application came in seeking a significant reduction in open space under the OHL lines, ACC would need to be satisfied that the development was still achieving high quality placemaking. Quality of open space was as important if not more important than quantity so one might achieve a better solution with less open space but of a higher quality. This was a matter of professional judgement. The design and access statement referred to in Ms MacArthur’s letter would indicate how loss of open space under the OHL might be compensated for, and this would require consideration. He did not disagree with anything which was said in the two letters, which indicated that ACC was comfortable with the principle of additional dwellings. His position was that he would be happy to contemplate extra residential units in the absence of the OHL, but the number would need to be worked upon. As he put it, there were two key requirements for compensation for loss of open space, namely, the children’s play area and the allotments on N2. There was also a certain value to the openness under the lines and he would expect some open space to be provided within new developed areas under the lines, to compensate for the whole loss. In openness he meant a recreational value. Leaving smaller areas of open space “pepper potted” within the developed areas could be one approach to compensation. ACC would be looking at compensatory provision for any space that would be lost. But Mr MacDonald could be expected to embrace the principles of the CDFMP in this connection.

[89] Mr Lewis’s comments were mainly directed at the N2 brief itself, which had implications for the north section of the OHL corridor beyond the N2 area itself. He was of course aware that the issues involved the southern section of the OHL. He was less familiar with the development framework for that area, and was non-committal, although agreed the matter of “openness” would be in play.

James Truscott – landscape architecture and masterplanning

[90] Mr Truscott spoke to his witness statement, his main report including a VIA dated October 2019, a rebuttal report dated December 2019 and a rebuttal statement of November 2020.

[91] Mr Truscott noted that the CDFMP categorised the Cults Burn corridor as neighbourhood open space whereas Hazleden Park and Wardhead Park were categorised as local open space, suggesting that the latter were within a lesser tier of importance in planning terms. Nevertheless the OHL corridor was an important north-south linkage. The linear space protecting the OHL corridor provided, in terms of the CDFMP, a range of local recreational uses, such as equipped play areas, allotments and kick about spaces for the local community. There was a bio-diversity element. The proposed OHL corridor provided an attractive setting for adjacent residential and potential employment areas. The corridor was part of a green link between Foggieton Woods in the south to the proposed tree planting area at N2. The corridor was intended as a location for “green” paths set off from the street, suitable for walking, cycling and equestrian use which connected to Core Path 57. Even if the connection to Core Path 57 were outwith the development site and the applicant’s control, a path could be run around the lobe of forestry to connect to the core path.

[92] Mr Truscott described the CDFMP as taking a positive and holistic view. Although the OHL was a landscape planning constraint, the open space underneath it could be turned into an opportunity, by creating an attractive place for local residents to enjoy and would provide wider benefit for the community as a whole. This was consistent with a theme of the CDFMP namely a design to create “a legible and clear urban form that has a unique sense of place and is highly attractive and pleasant as a community to live in.” He considered that the N2 Developer Brief appeared to play down the benefits of the OHL corridor and accentuated the negative aspects, which was the opposite of the development framework. The development had been promoted under the CDFMP as part of a “lifestyle choice”, built around the feeling of being in the countryside. As he put it, the principles established by the CDFMP would be completely undermined by the N2 brief.

[93] Mr Truscott pointed out that ACC’s requirements for open space were minimum requirements. He estimated that with the loss of the OHL corridor to development, there would be a reduced total of open space of 27.98ha, i.e. only about 7ha above the minimum requirement of 20.53ha. In his opinion this was not a generous provision of open space as suggested by the applicants. By way of contrast the nearby Grandhome development for 7,000 homes provide approximately 85ha of public space which is 40ha above the minimum requirement.

[94] Mr Truscott pointed out that no comprehensive review of the whole scheme had been carried out in the light of removal of the OHL corridor. It was not investigated, for example, whether new housing could not instead be provided elsewhere, such as upon the Cults Burn corridor. That corridor was essentially another physical constraint which had been incorporated into the masterplan as public open space. There was no suggestion in the N2 paper that there was potential to locate a greater amount of housing there despite the fact that Hazleden Park and Wardhead Park comprised much smaller areas. The CDFMP had promoted the OHL corridor open space equally with the Cults Burn corridor, and he did not agree that the latter had greater significance. He could not suggest that one corridor was more important than the other.

[95] We did not understand Mr Truscott’s final position to suggest that any of ACC’s technical accessibility requirements for open space would be contravened by the N2 brief or by development upon the southern portion of the OHL. However, Mr Truscott did consider there to be qualitative issues. Hazleden Park provided the only meaningful green space in the northern development area, so its loss would involve the loss of a green spine and thus amenity of the area would suffer. He adopted the point made by officers that there would result in “an amorphous mass of housing,” and the same comment could be made for the southern OHL corridor should it be removed. The proposed play area at N13 was not very far away from Hazleden Park but was smaller. The linear form of the northern section of the open space served to break up housing, which helped to provide the rural feel of placemaking there. He would be reluctant to split allotments since allotments required infrastructure and required to be accessible to people. He could concede, reluctantly, that the allotments in the north section could in theory be provided under the OHL at the west of the site. Both Hazleden Park and Wardhead Park were worthy of their location in his view. The latter was a more informal park with a small play zone. There was not a huge matrix of parks, as he put it, adjacent to Hazlehead Park (by which we understood he included Hazlehead Woodlands) and he did not accept Wardhead Park could be replaced without compensation. He was prepared to accept that some low density housing might be possible on the central area of the OHL corridor, but would like to see some form of green linkage remain there. He did not think that tree lined streets were an appropriate replacement for the large open corridors. Should housing be provided on the OHL corridor, the ripple effect elsewhere would mean root and branch rewriting of the masterplan.

[96] Mr Truscott considered that OPEN’s statement that the OHL would result in a considerable impact to residents was overstated. He developed a theme that the OHL (and two others) were part of the existing landscape and newcomers would accept them as they will have known nothing else when they move in. ASH prepared a VIA which was carried out over a study area of 100m on either side of the OHL, in areas N2, N3, N4 and N13. It had been provided under reference to the guidelines for landscape and visual impact assessment by the Landscape Institute 3 rd edition (“GLVIA 3”). He had been assisted by an experienced colleague. The study considered 34 groups of houses as receptor locations. The VIA found that in the first year there would be no “major” or “moderate-major (significant)” adverse effects arising from the OHL, and that only 17% of the residential receptor locations would experience “moderate (significant)” effects on visual amenity. Of the total, 48% were found to be either minor or negligible with the balance of 35% being minor-moderate adverse (not significant). The building location, juxtaposition and orientation in relation to the OHL were found to be the main sources of mitigation of adverse effects. The effects were found to be less after 15 years. The significantly affected receptor locations for both first year and 15 years lay within 20m and 35m of the OHL, i.e. a maximum of 15m outside the OHL corridor, which was effectively 10m less than the “outer transmission corridor” shown in Plan 2.

[97] Mr Truscott accepted that the LVIA guidance assumed the carrying out of a fairly high level study. However it was possible for there to be an “add on” section in respect of private residential amenity. He accepted that he gave more value for views from the front of houses and did not consider views from within a property’s curtilage or from a road as might affect the setting. Many of the receptors were assessed with “low” sensitivity because of a property’s orientation. A “medium” magnitude of visual change was assessed on the basis that “the OHL would occupy a noticeable part of the existing view.” Not all visual changes which were assessed as “medium” resulted in a significant impact.

[98] Turning to the montage provided by OPEN, it should be borne in mind that there would be screen planting between the receptors and the pylon, perhaps involving a double row of semi-mature trees. Other views would be screened by buildings. He thus defended the study result that viewpoints from groups 12 and 14 were not assessed as “significant.”

Steven Black - planning

[99] Mr Black spoke to his witness statement, his main report dated October 2019, a rebuttal report dated December 2019 and a rebuttal statement dated November 2020. He also referred to a planning report dated November 2017 and a rebuttal report dated February 2018 referred to in the necessary wayleave proceedings.

[100] In summary Mr Black did not consider that the OHL corridor land would have been granted planning permission for additional residential development as at the relevant date. Furthermore, as at the relevant date the corridor land did not even have the benefit of PPiP for residential development. Nor did the corridor land have designation for residential development in terms of the CDFMP which formed adopted SG at the relevant date.

[101] Mr Black put weight on the fact that the reporter in the necessary wayleave applications concluded that the PPiP did not allow the development of housing on the OHL land. Moreover without an amendment to the adopted CDFMP a planning application as envisaged by the applicant would be at risk of refusal as contrary to the development plan, since the CDFMP was itself SG and thus part of the development plan. The view that removal of the OHL would be a material consideration was debateable and would depend upon more information, and a final view by ACC in the light of consultation responses of the public and statutory consultees. It would be necessary to consider the impact which the loss of open space would have on the wider site, whose value could be seen from the terms of the CDFMP itself.

[102] A theme of Mr Black’s evidence was that it would not be possible to seek permission to develop under the OHL via the PPiP, because in his opinion, the PPiP was tied to the ES and various development blocks which were part of the available information at the time of the application. The OHL corridor was outwith the blocks identified for development in the supporting information. The conditions attached to the PPiP made numerous reference to “blocks” of development, which unlike the references to “phases” identified the locations for development, and without block details the conditions would be meaningless. Condition 25 referred to all works being carried out in accordance with the summary of environmental commitments specified in the ES. In his opinion various matters specified in the ES were zone specific and he disagreed with Mr Lewis on the flexibility of the zones.

[103] Mr Black adopted ASH’s view that the open space corridors were a fundamental design principle which would be completely undermined by the N2 brief, which gave no clarity on how landspace elements and functions could be accommodated elsewhere on the wider site. He went over the N2 discussions in detail. The letters in question had no status, they merely represented an officer view of the option in question. He was somewhat bewildered that the OHL “Option b” was tacked on, so to speak, at the end of the document. He detected, as he put it, a degree of nervousness by the officers in the correspondence who were being put under time pressure by being sent chasers, and who ultimately received a “reassuring” email from CDL that the discussions were not being treated as a planning application. Mr Beattie did not seem to have been aware that it was being suggested that open space would be removed, whose position would otherwise have been expected to have been entirely different. It would be for development control officers to consider whether land was not still required for open space.

[104] The fact that the officers wished to see a design and access statement suggested that ACC, although showing willingness to consider an alternative layout to the CDFMP, did not have a final position on N2. He would have wanted to see details to consider the “wave” effect as he put it created beyond the OHL corridor. He would have wished to see how “amorphous” housing could have been avoided and how open space requirements would be unaffected. Overall ACC’s response to N2 gave limited comfort to a developer.

[105] Mr Black accepted that a prospective purchaser of the OHL land would wish to know officer’s views on prospects for development in a no scheme world. No particular planning policy or issue had changed between the relevant date and the date of the second ACC letter in April 2019. It would be the case that in 2018 the CDFMP would have been more recent and thus would be given more weight. He did not make a case that ACC’s open space requirements would be breached if the OHL corridor were to be developed, but he agreed with Mr Truscott that there were qualitative issues to be addressed.

[106] Mr Black struggled with the idea that there could be “betterment” with removal of the OHL if all the open space under the corridor were to be lost. Some logic would be required in order to be allowed to depart from the CDFMP as adopted SG.

[107] Turning to the central area of open space in the OHL corridor, he accepted Mr Truscott’s position that this area was not required, in general terms, for quantitative or qualitative open space.

[108] In the event of some form of application to develop the OHL corridor for housing, there would most likely need to be a consultation exercise and committee decision. There would need to be amendment to the CDFMP. Without adequate compensatory open space, there would be a significant risk to gaining approval. Having regard to earlier representations commenting upon the benefit of Hazleden Park, there was a risk that SNH could object. The ES referred to the open spaces and thus did not assume development at these locations, and so might require amendment. There was also a risk a community council might object since there was an element of “giving them what they wanted but taking it away again.” He felt there was a risk that ACC members would raise concerns about the loss of parkland. He did not see evidence of compensation for the loss of open space.

[109] Mr Black considered there was no developmental plan shortfall in housing which would require the OHL corridor to be developed. However, he acknowledged Mr Findlay’s efficiency and density argument, which he had not mentioned in his written evidence.

[110] He also considered that the likely timescale associated with an application to amend the PPiP or make an application for full planning permission would take about 12 months assuming a review of the ES was not required.

[111] Mr Black’s final position was that the prospects of success for an appropriate application for planning permission for residential development on the OHL corridor would be about 15% in a no-scheme world. In respect of the central area he would assess this at about 20%.

Eric Shearer - valuation

[112] Mr Shearer spoke to his witness statement, his main report dated October 2019, a rebuttal report dated December 2019 and a supplementary report dated September 2020.

[113] Mr Shearer approached the valuation of the OHL corridor, assuming full development value, by means of a direct comparable method, as opposed to a residual valuation exercise which had a large number of unknown variables. Essentially the appropriate method would depend upon how far one was along the development curve. The comparable method could comprise a rate per acre or a unit or coverage rate per acre. As a local agent he was aware of the Mains of Countesswells transaction. He would give this a great deal of weight since it comprised part of the development site and had been concluded by parties after a fair amount of negotiation. Unlike the agreed table between Mr Court and Mr Stevens, Mr Shearer tended to value development in terms of gross acres. Although property developers were only interested in net acres, he acted for farmers who tended to feel they would be “selling land for nothing” unless gross acreages were referred to.

[114] On the question of hope value, Mr Shearer thought that any purchaser of the OHL corridor land would be at risk from CDL. CDL had extensive control over the area. As he put it CDL could make life very difficult for any buyer trying to obtain consent on a competing site. There was also a family who owned the largest part of the remaining 20% of the land at the west of the masterplan area. They could take steps to ensure they did not lose any of “their” allocated units in the CDFMP.

[115] Mr Shearer expressed some surprise at the content of the two ACC letters from Mr Beattie and Ms MacArthur. He would want to know how high up in the pecking order, as he put it, the officials were. However, he appeared to accept that Mr Beattie was an influential figure within ACC and if the letter in question concerned Mr Beattie’s “patch”, he would have to give it weight.

[116] He accepted whether or not there was PPiP for a particular development would be a major consideration in assessing hope value.

[117] Mr Shearer referred to two transactions in which a “bottom up” approach to hope value was reflected in the transaction. The first was Cloverhill Farm in Bridge of Don. The land had planning consent for business use. The buyer had felt there was a 40% chance of planning success for residential use. This eventually came to fruition. The price paid for the land reflected approximately 5% of the ultimate consented value. The Cloverhill transaction also involved a ransom strip which was dependent upon the future de-trunking of the AWPR.

[118] The other comparison was a site at Culter House Road. The existing use was forestry. The purchaser acquired the site in 2012 and managed to sell a portion of it in 2019 having been granted planning permission for residential use. The initial purchase price was of the order of 8% of the ultimate selling price. The ultimate selling transaction may have included an overage provision.

[119] Mr Shearer considered that these sites were more likely to have obtained planning permission for housing than the OHL corridor. In general terms hope value would be assessed on a “bottom up” principle, where the downside is limited. If as in the present case there was a 20% possibility of planning permission for residential use, it meant there would be an 80% chance of failure. Thus the development prospect would be quite difficult to get anyone to look at seriously. In general terms the purchaser would be taking on a planning fight. He would value the hope value of the corridor at £5,000 per acre say £50,000 in total.

[120] Mr Shearer considered that the Barratt 2 transaction to be different to the hypothetical OHL land sale, since the land which Barratt had purchased had been masterplanned, there was infrastructure in place and could be built within a reasonably short period of time.

[121] Mr Shearer did not have experience in injurious affection claims for OHLs, but is a very experienced agent. He agreed diminution in value could occur in certain cases, but not here. Mr Shearer’s main report made reference to the Dandara site at Grandhome, as discussed in Mr MacLeod’s evidence. A bid made for this site 30m from the OHL was in excess of the price paid 14 months earlier for land 190m away from the OHL, and was not the highest. In his view he did not think there was a falling market between the relevant dates in 2017 and 2019; prices were stable or rose slightly in that period.

[122] He referred to evidence from Dandara about the development site at Oakfields, Hazelwood where it was not believed that OHLs to the south of the site have had an impact upon sales. He accepted that his report making reference to the table of properties at the Dandara site in an appendix was incorrect. All the “Rowan” type properties shown by the appendix plan were in fact over 45m away from the OHL, and contrary to his report none were within 45m. However, a more recent plan showed the existence of three further Rowan type properties, plot numbers 33, 34 and 35. Although these had not been constructed when he visited the site, their footprint had been marked out. He was able to pace out, and, since there was a site barrier obstructing him, estimate the distance between these future units and the OHL. He also used a ruler on his Google map screen facility. Number 35 was within 45m of the OHL and had sold for the same price as the more distant No. 33. Both were “end of terrace” properties and had been sold during 2021. He did not accept that the injurious affection chapter in his report was misleading.

[123] Another unit, plot No. 4, had sold at a higher price and was further away from the OHL, but this had been a show home with higher specifications and a mature garden. Mr Shearer, however, accepted there was a certain incongruity regarding the sale of Rowan type houses in the proximity; for example, plot No. 28 sold for a significantly lower price than others on the same street and with an apparently similar outlook to the OHL: i.e. No. 28 sold for £399,950 in May 2019 whereas No. 29 next door sold for £442,950.

[124] Mr Shearer had not investigated the planning position. He had not mentioned the fact that Dandara had sought a quotation for the cost of undergrounding the OHL at Oakfields, and did not appear to accept that the purpose of doing so might involve considering a consequent increase in the value of houses to be built outwith the no build zone.

Eric Stevens - valuation

[125] Mr Stevens spoke to his witness statement, his original report dated October 2019, a rebuttal report dated December 2019, a supplementary report dated September 2020, and a rebuttal statement of November 2020.

[126] A strong theme in Mr Stevens’ original report was that the applicants had sustained no loss. CDL had acquired the land in April 2016, in the full knowledge of the existence of the OHL and the fact that the CDFMP had designed the development around the OHL. The grant of the necessary wayleave did not therefore cause any loss of development value. This remained Mr Stevens’ position. He did not think a “windfall” could be categorised as a loss.

[127] In Mr Stevens’ opinion development value should be assessed on the basis of the comparable evidence, with a residual appraisal calculation as a backup. The four comparables on the agreed table, excluding the second Barratt transaction as being post-relevant date, showed a compelling picture of uniformity. On the basis of the comparable evidence of headline values (prior to deduction of section 75 costs and strategic infrastructure costs), he would assess that private housing land would be valued at £1,155,631 per acre. We understood this to be a weighted average of 3 of the comparables, but not Mains of Countesswells whose details were not initially available. As a blended rate including affordable housing, and after relevant deductions, this would amount to approximately £784,000 per acre. The latter figure would compare with his residual valuation of £815,047 per acre. He had initially looked at both methods equally, but now preferred the comparable approach on account of details of the Mains of Countesswells transaction being made available.

[128] There was a big difference between his approach and Mr Court’s approach as to the apportionment of affordable housing land. This is noted in box 5 of the Scott Schedule but is relevant to both comparative and residual assessments. Mr Stevens’ density figure of 14.10 affordable dpa was based on an analysis of the Mains of Countesswells sale which adopted a ratio of 80:20 private/affordable. This would involve semi-detached or terraced houses. Mr Court’s figure of 23 affordable dpa resulted in only 12.5% of the site being allocated for affordable housing. Mr Stevens did not accept that his resultant figure of 11.36 private dpa was a particularly low density in relation to other metrics. The higher affordable density presented by Mr Court was based upon flats being built in the centre of the development whereas the OHL corridor would in reality be more spread out. Mr Court’s approach implied land being sacrificed in the centre of the site for affordable housing which would require compensation elsewhere in the calculation.

[129] Turning to other matters within the Scott Schedule, he did not think his figures for house footprint (box 6) and ultimately for site coverage were low; he considered them to be perfectly normal. There was also a significant difference between experts on sales revenue per square metre (box 7), in which his figure was based upon the sales evidence.

[130] Mr Stevens agreed that Mr Court’s residual valuation was significantly out of line with the comparable evidence. He did not think it could be explained simply by one developer seeking a higher profit on GDV. One could not take the contrary opinion of only one house builder where in his experience the 20% allowed for was adequate.

[131] Dealing with the comparative approach, Mr Stevens thought that applying a rate per acre was a sensible approach as the comparables were good. He did not think that there were particular advantages at the OHL location compared to other parts of the Countesswells development. He noted that in the comparable table the sites sold with a higher or lower private density still produced a very similar rate per acre. He did not think that a more generous figure than that derived from the table was appropriate on account of the large Barratt 2 transaction. The 468 units sold might take 13 or 14 years to sell; that housebuilder would be unlikely to need additional land for the foreseeable future. One bulk sale did not imply additional demand, there would always be an average number of sales and it appeared there had been no sales for private land in 2019. He contended that the 10% discount from the price in the Mains of Countesswells transaction took account of the fact there would be a 5 or 6 year delay before properties would be brought to market and sold.

[132] On the basis of planning advice Mr Stevens had only valued 3.19 acres (1.29ha) (this area has been subsequently corrected to 1.82ha) representing the central part of the OHL corridor. This was a very small proportion of the whole development area controlled by the applicants – of the order of 0.78% - it was therefore very difficult to support an argument that the “loss” of this area had any impact upon the overall capacity of the Countesswells site or resulted in significant loss to the claimant. Moreover, in his opinion any loss would only arise once all the land in the applicants’ control had been sold. The additional OHL land was essentially a windfall. It could only be regarded as producing an “additional” receipt once the rest of the development had been sold off. Any development on the OHL land would simply be a displacement of the existing phasing; value was only added to the applicants’ development by the hypothetical OHL land, at the very end of the development. If the Countesswells site reached maturity before additional receipts could be generated, there would be no loss. In his opinion, allowing for a full build out at the rate of 120 private homes per year, the applicant might be in a position to benefit from additional land in 14.5 years’ time. Accordingly any “loss” derived from the inability to develop the OHL corridor should be discounted at a rate of 5% per annum for that period. Based on a full site value of £2,600,000 for 3.19acres, the discounted figure would be £1,300,000.

[133] Mr Stevens defined hope value as an assessment of what a purchaser might pay for land without the benefit of a residential planning permission in principle, but the hope that one might be secured. Development value was where an assessment would conclude there was a certainty of planning permission in principle. A “top down” approach for hope value would only be appropriate if prospects of success were at least 50%. If as Mr Black indicated prospects of planning permission were so limited, i.e. to be within a range of 15-20% of success, in his opinion a “bottom up” approach would be appropriate. This would be of the order of £10,000-15,000 per acre, i.e. about two or three times agricultural value. He settled on a figure of £108,500 being broadly two times agricultural value. He accepted that if the main infrastructure required for development was already in existence, this would reduce cost and risk. He also accepted that if Mr Black was wrong in stating that the OHL corridor was not covered by the PPiP for residential use, this would make a significant difference to his view.

[134] Turning to the injurious affection claim, Mr Stevens made the point in his first report that the considerable volume of research studies show mixed results. Some cases are contradictory, with some reporting significant negative impacts while others find no correlation between a house’s proximity to power lines and a decrease in value. He pointed out that the Sims and Dent study is 18 years old and concerns sales 25 years ago. House designs have changed since. The OHL in question was a 275 kV line running through Blackwood, Cumbernauld and is thus a larger piece of infrastructure. The report refers to research from the US where power lines are generally situated in a right of way corridor, meaning that property adjacent to the right of way has the benefit of the extra land. At the time in the UK there was no general right of way corridor and property could be built directly beneath the power lines.

[135] Mr Stevens’ report referred to Mr Shearer’s written evidence about the Grandhome Oakfields development used as comparables, and also refers to ASH’s landscape and visual report. The latter refers to the visual effect mitigation techniques employed by the applicants. Nevertheless on balance Mr Stevens initially considered there was potential for the OHL to have a negative impact upon the value of homes close to both overhead lines and towers. He considered there to be a house price discount to value of 10% for houses less than 45m from a pylon and a 5% discount for properties less than 25m from the no build corridor (i.e. lying within the outer 25m corridor.) In his view diminution in value would tend to be plot specific in context.

[136] Mr Stevens carried out residual value calculations using an appraisal of a hypothetical 5 acre development plot. A sensitivity analysis indicated that a diminution in value of 10% of average house sales produced a loss in development land value of £280,000 per acre. A diminution of 5% in house sales produced a loss in development land value of £140,000 per acre. He revised his figures after having discussions with Mr MacDonald about the acreages within the 25m outer zone. There remains a dispute in that Mr Stevens does not include areas of distributor roads within the outer zone blocks. There is also a dispute whether a particular part of area N13 is affected, since it is a mixed use block including commercial and retail property whose value is unlikely, in his opinion, to be affected. If one took account of the northern area by including only 50% of block N13, because the mix would include residential, Mr Stevens calculated a reduction in value to the northern land by £432,627. He calculated a diminution in the southern area by £305,042. He then applied a discount to the northern “loss” to estimate the timing of the loss by assuming the properties would be sold 2 years after the valuation date (i.e. in 2020), and by a period of 5 years in respect of the southern section. He applied a discount rate of 5% per annum. This reduced the northern section loss to £392,406, and the southern loss to £239,009. Thus the total loss would be £631,414. If the N13 mixed use area is excluded altogether his figure would be £599,735.

[137] Mr Stevens did not consider there to be any deduction in value for affordable housing land on account of the OHL. JLL’s in-house social housing team had given advice as to the existing use value for social housing (“EUV-SH”). This was disconnected from the vacant possession value of the unit. The calculation is based upon rental income, which in turn derives from current affordable housing supply programme (AHSP) grant levels which dictate what a registered social landlord can afford to pay for a housing unit. So long as there is a suitable demand for social housing at Countesswells, the proximity of the units would have little or no bearing on the rent driven cash flow. His calculations assumed that 20% of the housing land would be for affordable housing and thus unaffected in value.

[138] Mr Stevens’ rebuttal report of December 2019 continued to accept there would be some degree of pricing impact for private homes close to the OHL and towers. However, in his witness statement Mr Stevens observes that Mr Shearer’s evidence has been supported by a witness statement from Mr Neil MacLeod, former land director at Dandara. Mr MacLeod refers to “there was no discernible difference in value for the same house type when you looked at the proximity to the overhead lines” at the Hazelwood development, and “there was no discernible difference in value attributable to the units backing up on to the overhead lines and we used the Hazelwood sales information as a basis for this approach to valuation at Grandhome.” Mr Stevens considered that Mr MacLeod’s testimony was “compelling.” Accordingly, and reflecting upon the evidence of ASH previously referred to, he was no longer of the opinion that there was a meaningful reduction in land as a consequence of the proximity of the OHLs. He described his earlier view as having been subject to “subconscious bias.”

[139] If Mr MacLeod’s evidence was not correct, he accepted that he would need to review his original position, but he did not concede that his original position (as arithmetically adjusted) was now inappropriate.

Submissions and Discussion

First claim – the law

[140] The applicants referred to Wyness v Scottish Hydro Electric Power Distribution plc where the Tribunal had discussed the authorities on paragraph 7(1) cases under Schedule 4 to the Electricity Act 1989. Counsel adopted the approach that the measurement of loss is a diminution in market value of the land, which in turn equates to the difference between the value of the land unencumbered and encumbered by the OHL. Compensation was for the loss which arises from the effective deemed imposition of the OHL on land which could otherwise have been developed. The claim was for hope value of the OHL corridor, but in the unusual circumstances of there being a valid and effective planning permission in principle for housing there. This was a case which merited no percentage deduction from full development value or, at least a very limited one. The issue was not whether housing would be permitted as a matter of principle, but in reality how much additional housing would be allowed. We were referred to Strang-Steel v Scottish Ministers as a reference to the Tribunal’s discussion of hope value in a compulsory purchase context. Counsel also referred to Arnold White Estates Limited v National Grid plc where the Court of Appeal said at paragraph 25:

“The grant put it out of the ability of the owner to turn his interest in the pylon land into money, either by selling it to a developer, or by developing it himself and selling the homes, once built, to residential occupiers.”

[141] The respondents accepted that the correct approach to establishing any diminution in value had been set out in Wyness and supporting cases, namely Brickkiln Waste Limited v Northern Ireland Electricity and McKibben v Northern Ireland Electricity .

[142] The respondents accepted that the valuation date is the date of the grant of the wayleave: Arnold White Estates paragraph 13. The general principles applicable to payment of compensation for compulsory purchase apply to claims under both sub-paragraph (1) and (2) of paragraph 7 of Schedule 4: Welford v EDF Energy Networks (LPN) Limited paragraph 14. This includes the principle of equivalence: Arnold White Estates paragraph 14. It was accepted that a hope value claim falls within the ambit of paragraph 7(1): Scottish Hydro Electric Transmission plc v Auquhirie Land Co Ltd . It was contended that an applicant’s loss might not necessarily be equivalent to a loss in market value of only part of an applicant’s heritable property. The reported cases emphasise that it is by reference to the value to the owner of the land being acquired that compensation is quantified, rather than (if different) its objective market value. The concept of value to the owner may in some circumstances produce less compensation than would be quantified by reference to open market value: Arnold White Estates Limited paragraphs 26-28. Reference was also made to Director of Buildings and Land v Shun Fung Ironworks Limited whereby a claim for losses require to satisfy the conditions of causation, remoteness and reasonable mitigation.

[143] The respondents reminded us that the price which the land in question might reasonably be expected to fetch on the open market would be expected to reflect whatever development potential the land has: Secretary of State for Transport v Curzon paragraph 27. In the case of hope value, it was not permissible to transform a probability of planning permission into a certainty of planning permission, since there must be a discount to reflect uncertainty: Transport for London v Spirerose paragraph 8. If statute directs that property is to be valued on an open market basis as at a certain date, one would not expect counterfactual assumptions to be made other than those that are inherent in the valuation exercise (such as the assumption that the property has been on the market and is subject of a sale agreement on the valuation date) or those which are directed by statute: Transport for London v Spirerose paragraph 50.

[144] A related theme is that things are to be taken as they are in reality on the valuation date, except to the extent that the instrument postulating the hypothetical transaction requires a departure from reality. It has been described as the principle of reality. The valuer should depart from reality only when the hypothesis so requires: Secretary of State for Transport v Curzon paragraph 42. This gives rise to a “reality principle” by which events which post-date the valuation date cannot generally be taken into account – it is a perception of future possibilities that matters. If the value of land can only be established by reference to the knowledge that the market would have had at the valuation date, post-valuation date events are necessarily excluded. Thus in assessing hope value, a value based on the hope of a future event occurring cannot be established by reference to post-valuation events showing whether such hope was or became more likely to be fulfilled: Secretary of State for Transport v Curzon paragraphs 54-55. This was different in the case of post-review date comparable transactions, where applying the presumption of continuity, there is a legitimate basis for an inference that a transaction on similar terms would have taken place at an earlier date.

[145] The foregoing propositions were not disputed although parties were in dispute as to how these principles fell to be applied. The respondents’ main submission was that at the valuation date, the evidence indicated that the market would not have attached any hope value to the applicants’ land in the OHL corridor, even if the OHL was not there. We agree that the question of hope value is the central issue to the first claim.

[146] We now turn to parties’ competing submissions. As with the written evidence these are extensive – the respondents’ written closing submission alone is of the order of 115 pages – so we mean no disrespect to the diligence of counsel when we only seek to record these here in outline.

Witnesses

[147] There were mutual attacks upon the other parties’ witnesses suggesting that they were not reliable, or in some cases not credible. The applicants submitted that the respondents’ witnesses had determinedly set their face against the claim for flawed reasons. The respondents’ pleadings and Mr Stevens had adopted a “no actual loss” argument on the basis that CDL had paid a price for the land which reflected no expectation of residential use under the OHL. Certain of the respondents’ witnesses had described the claim as a “windfall,” which description was pejorative. The “no loss” argument did not stand scrutiny against the authorities but had only been dropped by not being advanced in the closing submissions.

[148] The applicants further submitted that Mr Black had questioned the bona fides of the applicants’ position that they had been unaware of the potential to seek removal of the OHL while they designed the development. His aspersions were unfounded in the light of the applicants’ evidence that they had been unaware of the position, and the evidence of Mr MacDonald who would have preferred the OHL to have been removed but had been told it could not be.
