It would not make sense for the applicants to spend money on designing the project around the OHL if they had thought that it could have been removed without cost to themselves. Mr Black is an experienced planner but also appeared to be straining to diminish the prospect of planning permission by incorrectly arguing that the PPiP restricted the use of the land under the OHL to non-residential use. Mr Truscott regarded the CDFMP to be determinative and could not accept that it was illustrative, despite the latter being stated in the document. Mr Truscott and Mr Black sought to convert detailed design points into over-arching principles which, they contended, required to be followed come-what-may. Mr Black was unable to take the ACC evidence at face value and along with Mr Truscott was not prepared to accept that the ACC officials had greater insight into the whole process than they had. The respondents’ witnesses placed considerable store on the reporters’ conclusions that the OHL corridor did not have planning permission for residential development, but failed to appreciate she was considering a different question and had quite different material available to her.

[149] The applicants further submitted that Mr MacLeod’s evidence could not be relied upon. His evidence about the Oakfields/Hazelwood transactions had been given without any concern to its accuracy, in the knowledge it would be used to inform Mr Shearer’s reports. He had omitted to mention that Dandara had considered undergrounding the OHL despite the fact that the latter’s design statement indicated that the pylons “dominate” the site in question. Mr Shearer’s evidence was unreliable and his report as to injurious affection containing inaccurate measurements was seriously misleading. Instead of admitting his error he sought to introduce fresh evidence on the morning of his evidence, ostensibly for “updating” his position. Nor had he investigated the planning position behind the examples upon which he was relying. Mr Stevens only gave one reason for changing his evidence as to injurious affection, which was the witness statement of Mr MacLeod. His reluctance to revert to his original position in the light of the inaccurate evidence of the Dandara transactions was surprising and undermined his evidence.

[150] The respondents criticised the applicants’ evidence. Mr MacDonald should not be given weight on planning matters. He had been intimately involved with the creation of the CDFMP over a number of years, thus Mr Truscott’s interpretation should be preferred as being more objective. He did not have suitable expertise to comment upon the ASH VIA. His colleague Mr Welsh who had assisted him should have been called as a witness. Similarly Mr Findlay could be contrasted with Mr Black in that the former had represented the interests of the applicants since 2012, and his close involvement in the Countesswells project meant he could hardly be described as independent. Various alleged inconsistencies in Mr Findlay’s reports were drawn to our attention. Weight should be given to the fact that Mr Shearer was a very experienced Aberdeen agent who had unique insight into how participants in the Aberdeen land market would have behaved. There were serious concerns as to whether Mr Court’s evidence was independent and objective. He had been aware of the amount of the claims initially prepared by Mr Fitzsimons and the former’s detailed figures produced remarkably similar results. His methodology was flawed in that Mr Court did not place his valuation in the context of the applicants’ wider ownership and control, unlike Mr Stevens.

[151] It is all too apparent to us that parties have adopted particularly polarised positions in this case. We feel this has not been assisted by the financial claims quantified by Mr Court from an early stage. We found his reports to be lengthy, complex, containing errors and inconsistencies. Although often containing apparently persuasive reasoning his approach led to results which are out of proportion with the good comparable evidence which we are fortunate to have in this case. As shall be seen later, his resulting figures are excessive and we think his assumptions require to be treated with caution. The respondents on the other hand, through Mr Stevens, have persisted throughout the process in a “no loss” argument which was not advanced in the closing submissions. Standing back, the acquiring authority would have appeared to have set its face against the claim rather than to adopt a facilitating approach. So the stage was set for enduring litigation.

[152] As is so often the case, the expert witnesses brought their own perspectives to bear. They came up with very different conclusions despite the primary facts being fairly uncontroversial. We would only make a few specific comments. We thought Mr MacDonald was an impressive landscape architect and a good witness. We got the impression that he was trusted by ACC to produce good designs and that he had an effective working relationship with the MDC team. He was qualified to comment upon visual impact matters. We are not attracted by the suggestion that the applicants should have also called Mr Welsh. This would only add to the expense of the exercise, and, although not invoked by either party is contrary to the spirit of section 9(3) of the 1963 Act, which provides generally for one expert witness on each side unless otherwise directed. We thought Mr John Findlay to be a good witness despite the respondents’ criticisms of his reports. His reports had evolved with the production of more information and were, we felt in general, fair and balanced. We did not think that Mr MacLeod or Mr Shearer were reliable witnesses. Mr MacLeod did not impress us with his supposed knowledge of the Dandara transactions. We have no doubt that Mr Shearer is an effective and knowledgeable agent but, we regret to point out, we think his evidence about one of the Dandara transactions fell below the standard we would expect from an expert witness. This has coloured our view of the remainder of his evidence.

Initial issues – planning, hope value and valuation

[153] The respondents submitted that to establish any diminution in value as envisaged in Wyness , it was necessary for the applicants to establish the actual market value of their property at the relevant date, to establish a hypothetical market value on the counter-factual assumption that the necessary wayleaves had not been granted, and to demonstrate that the hypothetical value exceeded the actual value, the extent of the difference being the measure of the loss. We did not think the submissions went beyond this position, but thus there remains a suggestion that the claim should fail since the applicants had not strictly set out this approach in their valuation evidence. In particular, the implied criticism would seem to be that the applicants have not attempted to value all their property in the area, as a whole, “before and after” the coming into effect of the scheme. The applicants have simply presented their case on the basis that the OHL corridor would, had they been able to remove the OHL, have had hope value which it did not have in the “encumbered” with-scheme world.

[154] While the respondents’ submitted approach is no doubt one method of establishing a loss in appropriate circumstances, we do not think any of the authorities suggest it is the only approach for a compensation claim. The respondents’ position amounts to something of a gloss on paragraph 7. As summarised by Lord Collins in Transport for London v Spirerose Limited paragraph [89] “the aim of compensation is to provide fair financial equivalent for the land (or rights in land – our parenthesis) taken.” In Arnold White Estates compensation was for the loss of the ability of the owner to turn his interest in the pylon land into money. So where the loss of that ability can be measured by an estimate of hope value in the OHL corridor, which is absent in the with-scheme world, we do not see why the full rigour of respondents’ suggested approach is necessary. We accept, of course, that the respondents have other submissions that the applicants’ loss requires to be viewed in the context of their entire landholding, where there is said to be a timing issue. It seems to us that this point is essentially covered by the “value to the owner” principle, which we shall deal with later.

[155] We now turn to the assessment of the “unencumbered” value of the OHL corridor. This is directly related to the prospects of securing planning permission for residential development there in the no-scheme world. By way of background, the applicants set out a number of additional or complementary factors which would influence a hypothetical purchaser or developer at the relevant date. The factors related to development risk in general. In particular, there was long term secure funding for strategic infrastructure; there were no abnormal infrastructure risks; the cost of section 75 agreements with ACC was known; other developers had purchased land from CDL, as had housing associations; housing development was under way with a good number of buildings being sold, thus demonstrating that the Countesswells development was attractive, and had won national awards and commendations; densities had been established by development that had taken place; and over-arching design principles were in place. It was clear to any purchaser that there was a market for land at Countesswells demonstrated by the sales which had occurred. These points were not disputed.

[156] There were three specific disputes about the assessment of hope value, and it is convenient we deal with these at the outset. Firstly, a major dispute was whether the PPiP established the principle for housing on the OHL corridor. The PPiP grants planning permission for a “residential led mixed use development including approximately 3,000 homes …” subject to (numerous) matters to be approved via formal MSC applications. The letter granting PPiP expressly refers to plans which on examination only contain the red line boundary.

[157] However, the respondents submitted that this did not legally commit ACC to the principle of housing development on the OHL corridor. Reference was made to Mr Black’s position. His view was that the PPiP was linked by condition (2) to specific development blocks, i.e. blocks which excluded the OHL corridor as could be identified in the CDFMP. It provided:

“(2) No development in connection with each respective phase/block of the planning permission hereby approved shall take place until full details of the siting, design, external appearance and landscaping within the relevant phase of the development … have been approved.”

[158] Since the conditions referred to “blocks” they would be meaningless without one being able to look at the background documents showing the extent of the blocks.

[159] Counsel referred to Trump International Golf Club Scotland Limited v Scottish Ministers and Lambeth LBC v Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government , in particular paragraph [34] from Lord Hodge’s judgment in the former:

“In summary, whatever the legal character of the document in question, the starting point – and usually the end point – is defined by “the natural and ordinary meaning” of the words there used, viewed in their particular context (statutory or otherwise) and in the light of common sense.”

[160] A common sense approach was required here and it was untenable to suggest that the PPiP was not tied to the SG when it is accepted that it forms part of the development plan. Condition 25 was also relevant since it required “works to be carried out in accordance with the summary of environmental commitments in Chapter 18 of the ES”, and the ES in turn showed the residential development areas being divided into blocks.

[161] The applicants submitted that the PPiP was simply a permission over all within the red line boundary. One could only look to documents extrinsic to the planning permission where there was lack of clarity. Reference was made to the passage of Lord Hodge in Trump International Golf Club Scotland Ltd at paragraph [33] referring to limited scope for the use of extrinsic material in the interpretation of a public document and, for example, Chelmsford City Council v Leisure Parks Real Estate (Holdings) Limited at paragraph 27(4). It was possible to read condition (2) without reference to any masterplan or design and access statement. It was not necessary at the “in principle” stage to know the details of the block in question. Condition (25) referring to the ES was only requiring works to be carried out in accordance with environmental commitments in that statement. Those commitments were not zone specific and the condition was not attempting to control the ambit of the permission. Moreover, there was no indication in the extensive discussions on N2 that ACC took the view that the PPiP precluded development on the OHL corridor. Mr Lewis had not thought that the ES commitments were zone specific.

[162] In our opinion the applicants’ submissions are to be preferred. Intuitively we would not have thought that a planning permission in principle would be tied to any particular design unless such were to be expressly stated in a condition. Condition (2) referring to “each respective phase/block” makes sense on its own on the understanding that the permission assumes it will be implemented in phases and blocks over time. This is consistent with condition (1) referring to a “detailed phasing programme outlining the delivery of buildings, open space and roads infrastructure across the entire application site” to be approved. The phasing programme, it can be inferred, would outline the buildings, roads etc. as would create the blocks to be delivered in due course. We do not think that the conditions need to be interpreted by a finding that there is a predetermined block or zone layout, only to be found in an extraneous document not mentioned by the condition. Equally we agree that condition (25) is not seeking to control the extent of the permission. It is only seeking to control the carrying out of the works.

[163] Moreover although chapter 18 of the ES is mentioned by the condition, we accept that the chapter is in general terms only. The ES is a very lengthy document, and the block plans are not to be found in chapter 18 in any event. So we do not think a common sense interpretation would lead one to think that the block plans are intended to be part of the PPiP. These points are underlined by the fact that in the discussions involving an enlarged N2 block the ACC officials did not give the PPiP the interpretation placed upon it by Mr Black. Nor was there any apparent issue over an earlier MSC application for an enlarged N6 and reduced N7 block. Indeed officials reporting on the application for PPiP stated that although the ES was submitted in support of the planning application it was not part of the application itself.

[164] Accordingly we conclude that ACC would have been obliged to deal with any MSC application proposing housing on the OHL corridor on the basis that the PPiP had established the principle of housing within the red line area generally. We accept it is theoretically possible that an MSC application might undermine or depart from some fundamental principle of a PPiP, and that a planning authority might therefore require a new application of some sort. However the N2 correspondence and Mr Lewis’ evidence did not indicate that this was a realistic scenario, and indeed the 3 April 2019 letter by Ms MacArthur suggested the making of a MSC, without mention of formal amendment of the CDFMP at all.

[165] Secondly, the respondents submitted that the N2 correspondence was irrelevant. In assessing hope value, post relevant date events could not be taken into account since it was only the perception of future possibilities that mattered: Secretary of State for Transport v Curzon , paragraphs 42-43 and 54-55. The N2 correspondence occurred after the relevant date and was, accordingly in general terms, irrelevant. The only basis upon which it might be considered was if at the relevant date the hypothetical purchaser would have acquired the same information as contained within the N2 correspondence as, for example, the result of a due diligence exercise. Reference was made to City & County of Swansea v Griffiths . That case made it clear that evidence was required in order to come to a conclusion as to the result of a due diligence exercise. The applicant had chosen not to adduce any evidence as to what investigations a hypothetical purchaser would have carried out, or what the results of any such investigations would have been. Only Mr Black had been asked if he were advising a potential purchaser of the OHL corridor were the OHL to be removed; counsel had asked Mr Black whether he would have gone to ACC and asked them for their view, to which Mr Black replied “absolutely”. Mr Black, however, did not accept that the response would have been as contained in one of the emails between ACC and Mr MacDonald. Mr Fitzsimons had indicated that the purpose of the N2 correspondence was to support the compensation claim and to take the place of a CAAD which was not available in the context of necessary wayleaves. The circumstances were therefore different from that of a hypothetical purchaser acquiring information from ACC through any due diligence exercise.

[166] The applicants reminded us that Mr MacDonald had indicated that he would have expected the same comments from ACC if the officers had been approached two years previously. The evidence did not suggest that there was any policy change within ACC between 1 August 2018 and the date of the N2 correspondence. The only conceivable changes were that at the relevant date the CDFMP was more recently adopted and might potentially be given more weight. However, the potential removal of the OHL in the hypothetical world could only be seen as a major change of circumstances. Also, the site was less developed as at the relevant date and thus there would have been fewer potential objectors. The applicants did not accept that Mr Fitzsimons had instructed the N2 correspondence purely as a means for compensation, rather it was to exert leverage to persuade the respondents to move the OHL. All the N2 correspondence had been properly addressing N2 as a planning issue.

[167] We think it is helpful to look at the full passage of Neuberger LJ in Swansea CC v Griffiths at paragraph 28:

“However it appears to me that it may have been legitimate to rely on the Tregof Farm planning permission (‘the 1998 permission’) on a slightly more indirect basis, along the following lines. A prospective purchaser of the land, when considering the likely attitude of the local planning authority to its residential development in 1996, might well have approached the planning officer for his assessment and advice. If evidence had been given to the member that that is the course that would have been taken by a prospective purchaser, then there may well have been a dispute as to what the reaction of the planning officer would have been. In my view, it would not, at least in principle, have been illegitimate in the circumstances for the respondents to have sought to rely upon the fact that, for some two years later, the planning authority was prepared to entertain, indeed to grant, residential planning permission for ‘piecemeal’ development on another site, namely Tregof Farm. The member would have been entitled, to conclude that, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the actual attitude of the planning authority in 1998 to housing development in the area was no different from the attitude which would have been communicated in 1996. Of course, whether or not such a conclusion would have been justified would have depended on the factual and expert evidence.”

[168] In our opinion the N2 correspondence does not fall foul of the “reality principle” for much the same reasons as given by his Lordship. The evidence indicates, entirely unsurprisingly, that the hypothetical purchaser would have been advised to approach planning officers familiar with the development for their views as to permitting development in a no-scheme world. The evidence suggests, and we accept, that there would have been little difference to a response to a query had it been made immediately prior to the relevant date (1 August 2018) or at the time of the latest N2 letter (3 April 2019).

[169] It also has to be borne in mind, in the present case, we are dealing very much with a hypothetical purchase since removal of the OHL is a hypothetical scenario. The applicants were advised that their objection would be unlikely to succeed in the necessary wayleave proceedings, as indeed it did not, and as far as we know the respondents have never come near to agreeing to remove or underground the OHL.

[170] As we said in Gordon v National Grid Gas plc paragraph 193, the hypothetical purchaser is assumed to act prudently and, in an appropriate case, would arm himself with necessary information in preparation of a development project. The background correspondence to N2 indicates that, at least ostensibly, the applicants were seeking an officer view on formal notepaper in order to “give future developers comfort”. In other words, in the eyes of ACC the applicants were assuming the role of potential seller and would wish to assist a potential purchaser with the natural question as to ACC’s likely position for development in the OHL corridor. In this connection we note Mr Lewis’ comment that his officers were dealing with a routine planning query involving changes in the layout of a large scheme. So it is the sort of approach which might have occurred in a no-scheme world.

[171] In these circumstances we do not think how exactly a hypothetical purchaser would have approached ACC can be judged too finely. For example, the N2 brief has been criticised by Mr Black for having insufficient detail. Conversely it and the correspondence has been criticised elsewhere as being lengthy and somewhat convoluted. It is unfortunate that there is no CAAD process available for cases such as the present. Such a process could have been used to go into much more detail as to what scale of development would in fact have been permitted in a no-scheme world. In reality a purchaser would cover itself by making suitable planning permission a suspensive condition for any purchase. As has been pointed out in numerous cases, this option is not available to the hypothetical purchaser, who is assumed to make a “clean” offer. The solution used here, to ask for an officer view, has the weakness that it is unlikely to result in any formal commitment as to a position of the council. But we still think the officer response is capable of evaluation.

[172] So taking account of all these factors, in our opinion the N2 correspondence fairly represents an approach which a hypothetical purchaser might have taken in carrying out due diligence prior to making an offer. It provides an initial general position which officers would have been likely to adopt. So we reject the respondents’ submission that the N2 brief and correspondence is irrelevant.

[173] The respondents advanced a third specific argument. The applicants’ case could be characterised as “all or nothing” because Mr Court, for example, had based his valuation for loss of development of the 128 houses on the basis that prospects were certain for planning permission. Mr Court had conceded that if this assumption was wrong, his valuation would need to be revisited and he had offered no alternative valuation based upon a lower percentage of success. While the Tribunal had the expertise to consider the relationship between prospects of success and hope value, as a matter of fair notice details of a lesser case had not been given to the applicants, assuming that prospects of success were judged to be less than 100%.

[174] The applicants referred to various passages in the pleadings to indicate that there was a fall-back position if planning prospects were judged to be less than certain. The pleadings contained the time honoured passage in which the applicants sought “… such other amount as compensation as the Tribunal may determine.” The statement of issues for the hearing submitted by the applicants contained the issue “whether CDL is entitled to compensation … for the loss of the opportunity to construct 128 dwellings (or such other number as the Tribunal may determine) …” The statement of issues submitted by the respondents contained “4(i) whether there was a 100% certainty of planning permission for 128 housing units or (ii) if not, what assessment the market would have made of the applicants percentage prospects of obtaining the necessary planning permission.” It was also pointed out that if say an expert witness had given a view there was a 100% chance of obtaining planning permission, it was difficult for him to address a lower chance if he did not agree with the assumption. Counsel also referred us to paragraph 56 in Wyness , where we had adopted a view expressed by Lord Elliott, the first Tribunal President, referred to in Rowan Robinson (paragraph 12.26 n. 220) to the effect that the Tribunal has something of an investigatory role in compensation claims.

[175] In our opinion in terms of the pleadings and various items of process, the evaluation of a claim based upon less than 100% certainty of success in planning, is fairly in play. The respondents have adopted a position that the planning prospects of success were no higher than 15% - 20%. The fact that there is little direct evidence commenting upon a middle ground of some sort is something of a function of the polarised views of parties’ witnesses. It is a familiar situation encountered by this Tribunal. If we do not find either parties’ polarised positions to be attractive, as indeed we do not, to some extent we will require to rely upon our own experience, always bearing in mind what can be inferred from the evidence.

Planning merits – applicants’ submissions

[176] We now turn to parties’ submissions as to the planning merits of the OHL corridor and how these would have been viewed by a hypothetical purchaser. The applicants submitted that Mr John Findlay’s confidence as to the prospects of residential development there was fully borne out. The site had planning permission in principle, the basis for the OHL corridor is presumed to have gone and due diligence would have ascertained that ACC accepted that “The open space created by the no-build zone is not a requirement of the development framework or masterplan in terms of design or place making ambitions”. This was an express passage stated in the N2 developer brief, and officers had not sought to gainsay it in discussions. Due diligence would have ascertained that ACC was not opposed to the principle of development on the corridor and were not seeking retention of any corridor. Properly understood the masterplan would have been recognised as being illustrative and not a straightjacket. Masterplanning guidance would have demonstrated how the site could have been developed in accordance with its over-arching principles. There was no basis for retaining the OHL corridor as undeveloped land.

[177] The applicants dealt with the issue whether ACC may have been reluctant to lose open space once provided, even if not required as such. It was suggested that the provision of open space under the OHL was not a matter of gain or loss but of attempting to do the best with the OHL. The relevant principles did not justify retaining open space without justification. The officials were concerned as to how open space requirements would be met, but Mr MacDonald had satisfied them, and Mr Lewis confirmed that pepper potting would have been a solution. Mr MacDonald confirmed that the proposed development is at a very low density and would allow ample provision to provide for pockets of open space, tree lined streets etc. which was consistent with the proposals elsewhere on site. ACC would also have had regard to guidance to make the most efficient use of land, as discussed by Mr Findlay, which approach was barely acknowledged by the respondents. It was submitted that it was clear from ACC’s responses that officers were unanimous in thinking that the replacement of the long linear park with well-designed residential development was a positive step. No “in principle” problems were raised that could not be satisfied. The officers had tested the principle of development under the OHL and were satisfied.

[178] The applicants pointed out that the respondents’ witnesses had been distinctly unwilling to acknowledge that the OHL corridor’s primary purpose was to provide for the OHL itself and that the open space uses were allocated to it in order to make some use of it. The background was not a dispute between the applicants and ACC with one party seeking more open space and the other less, so that if the OHL were to be removed ACC might seek to rely on an ostensible “gain”. On the contrary there was a common desire to produce high quality development. There was no recognition at any stage that such required a long linear park at the location. There was no “over provision” of open space, just a design which met the principles, but which would have been very different without the OHL. The respondents’ comments that the N2 paper undermined the CDFMP were wrong. Mr MacDonald had also contended that the masterplan was illustrative, not definitive, and this was a point of view which Mr Lewis appeared to accept, but not by the respondents’ witnesses.

[179] The applicants also pointed out that Mr Truscott had accepted that the OHL land could be fully developed for residential use without any breach of the specific open space requirements. Mr MacDonald had said that provided the play space and allotments were moved there would not be any breach of requirements, and Mr Truscott and Mr Black’s acceptance of this was not acknowledged in their written evidence. Mr Truscott was driven back to relying on a “green lung” type argument, but if such was important, he could not explain why there was no similar green lung on the north west side of the development or elsewhere. The OHL corridor did not connect anything of importance – save the pylons. Mr Truscott’s evidence was undermined by his insistence that the OHL corridor was of equal status to the Cults Burn corridor, which was not the case.

[180] It was accepted by the applicants that the masterplan had become part of the LDP and may need to be changed. This could be accomplished with relative ease in comparison with changing more important parts of the LDP. It was noted that not all masterplans become SG.

[181] The applicants submitted that, read fairly and sensibly, the N2 correspondence demonstrated that the ACC officers considered from a planning perspective (as opposed to a compensation perspective) both the implication of residential development in an extended N2 brief but also under the wider OHL corridor. Clearly they did not approve anything since there was nothing before them to approve. It was clear from the correspondence that this was about sounding out the officers, establishing the principle and whether there were any general issues that arose. The officers did raise issues including the amount of open space. The issue they raised as to “amorphous housing” was not in the context of retaining open space but ensuring new residential development was appropriately designed and integrated. Mr MacDonald made it clear that any in-principle issues were dealt with. It was also significant that a development control case officer was involved in the correspondence. Counsel underlined the passages in the ACC letters demonstrating that Mr Beattie for example was considering the whole OHL corridor and that open space provision was a matter of quality not quantity. Other passages indicated that Mr Truscott’s attempt to present the OHL corridor as a desired green lung or equivalent of strategic importance was not grounded in practical planning. There was no absolutely no suggestion in the correspondence of some need to keep any form of linear green park.

[182] The views of Mr Lewis were aligned with his team. There was no reason not to accept the N2 correspondence at face value in the absence of direct evidence from the officers involved.

[183] The applicants accepted that Mr Lewis did not have the detail for a final decision. The proposed changes could be argued as less significant than those changes to the development due to the new road, altered plot size and layout, reduction in size of the school and inclusion of new housing units and relocation of the mixed use which led to the CDFMP addendum in 2017. That was the sort of change which could be and indeed was accommodated by changes to the masterplan and by way of MSCs. The idea that SNH/NatureScot would object to the proposal as a matter of national importance was fanciful. The idea that a community council would oppose a loss of space which has yet to be provided, which it had already criticised, was stretching credulity.

[184] The applicants pointed out that in real life the purchaser would have secured an option, perhaps with an overage clause in favour of the seller. But in the present hypothetical world, circumstances justified a finding that there would have been a 100% certainty of residential development being permitted, or if not, at least an extremely high likelihood. Mr Shearer’s two examples of hope value were wholly different and the suggestion of a bottom-up approach to valuation should be rejected. The Mains of Countesswells transaction had a similar planning status but did not involve a bottom-up approach.

[185] The real question, the applicants submitted, was how many units would a hypothetical purchaser have based its offer on? It was submitted that in terms of numbers of units and size the applicants had been conservative. The applicants’ figures were consistent with what is proposed in adjoining parcels, and tie in with the N2 brief. Counsel also pointed out that the respondents’ witnesses appeared to accept that the central area of land could be developed, although Mr Truscott appeared to caveat his position by suggesting the need to retain a corridor of some unspecified width. The case could be distinguished from Strang-Steel because in that case there was no planning permission whereas here there was planning permission in terms of the PPiP. The principle is assured and the only issue was in terms of numbers and amount of land that would have been available for allocation. There was a defined allocation and planning permission in principle.

Planning merits – respondents’ submissions

[186] The respondents’ position was that a hypothetical purchaser of the OHL corridor would have assessed the chances of obtaining planning permission for houses at no more than 15 - 20%. There was no dispute that the OHL open space corridor including Hazleden Park and Wardhead Park were designated as local open space and included allotments and different types and sizes of play areas. The CDFMP was adopted SG and was therefore part of ACC’s LDP. The hypothetical purchaser acting reasonably would have regarded the planning outcome as far from certain on account of the importance of Hazleden Park and Wardhead Park within the scheme envisaged in the SG. Reference was made to Mr Truscott’s evidence pointing out the significance of the parks within the design principles of the CDFMP of which the landscape strategy was a key layer. If Hazleden Park were to be built upon “the green spine that brings the countryside into this semi-rural area would be taken away”, hence the need to avoid the “amorphous massive housing” referred to by the ACC officers. His position was similar in relation to the southern section of the OHL corridor should Wardhead Park be removed. The respondents further submitted that the extent of land uses under the OHL specifically adopted within Hazleden and Wardhead Parks would require to be relocated elsewhere within the masterplan site, and it would follow that the applicants’ remaining land holdings elsewhere would be reduced.

[187] Mr Truscott had pointed out the fact that the OHL corridor formed an integral part of the “access and connectivity strategy” and he had referred to the ES underpinning the development framework in respect of the connections in the development and wider area. There was a difference in terms of environmental mitigation between a green corridor of the type adopted in the SG, and a street lined with trees as suggested in the N2 brief.

[188] The respondents criticised Mr MacDonald’s evidence. He had not identified any specific location where the lost allotment space on his Hazleden Park design might be relocated. But the real question was not whether ACC would agree to open space changes. The question was to what extent a hypothetical purchaser would regard ACC’s agreement to changes as certain in a no-scheme world. Mr MacDonald’s confident assertion that he was certain an MSC application for the 10.85 acres would be approved by the council should be given limited weight. Mr Truscott’s interpretation of the CDFMP should be preferred since his more objective position was more akin to the position of the hypothetical purchaser. Mr MacDonald had not been clear how design principles that would be departed from could be addressed to the satisfaction of ACC. The issue went beyond merely ensuring that ACC’s minimum open space requirements were met, since if that were the case the lengthy N2 correspondence would not have been necessary, which correspondence in any event was inconclusive as an attempt to establish that a proposal would be acceptable to ACC.

[189] The respondents pointed out that Mr Findlay’s evidence was inconsistent with absolute certainty of planning permission in the no-scheme world. He had accepted that an amendment to the SG would be required which would need to cover the entire masterplan site in order to address the ripple effect. That would be a formal process potentially involving Scottish Ministers. Even if officers recommended approval of an amended masterplan, the council might not follow that recommendation. Councillors could, for example, be lobbied by an affected community council.

[190] Nor had Mr Findlay addressed the position of SNH/NatureScot which provided an example of uncertainty. SNH had supported the design principles of Hazleden Park including landscaping there to help wildlife corridors and benefit nature conservation. As he accepted SNH’s position would be a material consideration, he could not discount the risk of the latter being involved in the decision-making process.

[191] The respondents also pointed out that Mr Findlay had accepted there was no evidence of any change in housing requirements that might give rise to a need for additional housing. The reliance he placed on previous changes to the masterplan was unsound and could not be applied to Hazleden and Wardhead Parks. If the OHL were to be removed, the land could still be used for those parks. This was different to the case of the primary school, for example, where the education authority no longer needed part of the allocated space. It was not credible to state that the hypothetical purchaser would have ignored the risk of ACC still wishing Hazleden Park and Wardhead Park to remain along the green corridor.

[192] In these circumstances the respondents submitted that Mr Black’s evidence should be given more weight. The prospect for planning permission for residential development on all 10.85 acres of the OHL corridor was of the order of 10%. Mr Black had pointed out that the CDFMP regarded the open space as a very significant benefit to the proper planning of the area. ACC were duty bound to manage the development and any change to the contrary must be considered as contrary to the development plan and would be required to be justified. All the uses of the corridor in terms of accommodating allotments, play areas and green corridors for bio-diversity were supported by development plan policy. The open space corridor was part of the fundamental design principles providing a key part of the landscape strategy. The respondents endorsed Mr Black’s position that although the removal of the OHL would have amounted to a change in circumstances, there was no reason why this would by itself have justified the removal of the green space and uses to be provided. There would require to be a consultation exercise with a final decision being taken by an ACC committee. Mr Black expressed the opinion that there was a significant risk to gaining approval of the proposed change unless there was a clear environmental benefit, or a planning demand that outweighed the value of the allocated public parks, allotments/community gardens, outdoor sports area, large scale play zone and natural green space connections with green corridors as originally allocated.

[193] Mr Black had also emphasised the importance of the ES, and the various mitigation proposals specified there would be given significant weight. The ES provided an assessment of the proposed development as described in the CDFMP and it was important to have regard to it as a whole. Mr Black had pointed out there was a risk that SNH could object to any application to remove Hazleden Park. Community councils might object to the loss of Hazleden Park and Wardhead Park. In summary Mr Lewis’ evidence indicated that it emphatically could not be assumed that planning permission would have been granted and that much more detail would have been given before the “initial views” given by Mr Beattie and Ms McArthur could be progressed to a final position. It was emphasised that Mr Lewis had stated that in addition to the play space and allotments there was a certain “value to openness” in the sense that some open space would require to be provided to compensate for the whole loss.

[194] Turning to the weight to be attached to the N2 correspondence, if relevant, the respondents submitted that it was hearsay. There was no explanation as to why none of the authors of the ACC correspondence gave evidence. A negative inference should be drawn to the fact that the applicants had chosen not to produce the bulk of the correspondence leaving it for the respondents to do so. A full picture of the communications had not been presented.

[195] In any event the question was what the hypothetical purchaser would have made of the N2 correspondence. Mr Black’s position was that taking it into account, he would adjust his original assessment (10% - 15% chance of success) to 15% - 20% chance of success. Ms McArthur’s letter of 3 April 2019 was not a statement of the council’s final position, but an initial view of the masterplan team and had not been subject to public consultation. There was a lack of detail as to how the loss of open space would be compensated for. All it showed was there was a willingness on the part of the council to consider an alternative to the existing adopted layout.

[196] The respondents adopted Mr Shearer’s evidence and referred to the two speculative purchases at Cloverhill Farm and Culter House Road. In the former a 40% chance of obtaining residential planning consent equated to a 95% reduction from full development value. In the latter a prospect of 50% prospect of residential planning permission equated to a discount of 92% from full development value. Mr Shearer had considered that prospects in the current case were substantially less than in those comparables. Mr Stevens also referred to Strang-Steel v The Scottish Ministers in which a 50% chance of planning permission resulted in an 80% discount to full development value. If Mr Black’s opinion on prospects were to be accepted, a hypothetical purchaser would be unlikely to pay more than two or three times agricultural value.

Discussion on planning merits

[197] We think that an informed purchaser would have regarded the views of planning officials as critical to its assessment of the planning merits of development in the OHL corridor in the no-scheme world. As we have indicated, we think it is fair to evaluate the N2 brief and officers’ comments, which can be used as a starting point. The hypothetical purchaser would wish to arm itself with comfort as to ACC’s likely view on the matter, and whatever form that correspondence might have taken it can be inferred that the council’s position would not have been dissimilar to the broad statements made in the letters of 14 December 2018 and 3 April 2019. In the event of the hypothetical purchaser being the applicants themselves, the purchaser would have also been armed with the expertise of Mr MacDonald.

[198] We think that the two letters represent a genuine planning appraisal by the officers of the N2 brief in the no-scheme world. The letters were designed to be “standalone” so we do not think it critical that we have not heard directly from the authors themselves; the letters are necessarily caveated on the need for further detail and the officers, had they given evidence, would no doubt have similarly caveated their positions. We also think it is fair to regard the N2 correspondence as giving a steer for the development for the whole of the OHL corridor. The N2 area is only one zone at the northern OHL corridor, but for example the officers could not have commented upon this area alone without having given some consideration to the N13 area further to the south.

[199] We accept it is possible to infer from the correspondence and Mr MacDonald’s evidence that ACC would have been open to persuasion to permit the whole of the OHL corridor to development, without necessarily creating “new” open space elsewhere as a substitute. There is no suggestion that the officers took exception to the statement in N2 to the effect that the open space created by the no-build zone was not a requirement of the CDFMP in terms of design or meeting placemaking aspirations. The 14 December 2018 letter refers to Plan 3 indicating the potential site capacity should the overhead lines be removed – 138 additional homes – which in the officer’s view would present a “far more welcome approach to placemaking.” It is possible that even the 0.4ha substitute play area in N13 advanced by the brief could have been found without loss of housing overall since it might be taken out of allocation of open space elsewhere, given the “surplus” amount of open space throughout the development and the potential for “pepper potting” open space.

[200] However we do not think this is the only interpretation which could be taken of the N2 correspondence and the wider picture. As we said in Strang-Steel at [145] hope value can properly be assessed on a fairly conservative assessment of the chances of obtaining planning permission. The hypothetical purchaser would require to take a cold hard look at the planning risks and potential downside of making a clean offer. It would thus need to consider whether a less optimistic view of the position could be taken. That said, we wholly disagree with the description in the respondents’ evidence that the hypothetical purchaser would have been taking on a “planning fight”. The removal of the OHL could not be regarded as other than a material change of circumstances to the design position set out in the CDFMP. In that scenario we think it is clear that ACC officials were willing in principle to recommend or permit additional housing development on the OHL. The only serious question was how much compensatory open space (either in the OHL corridor or equivalent elsewhere) would have been insisted upon, thus affecting the potential amount of additional housing land.

[201] It is apparent that the officials did not regard the OHL green corridor as important as the Cults Burn corridor, we think for good reason. Mr Truscott’s position at times to the contrary suggests an overstatement in his position. The LDP treated the latter as part of a greenspace network, and we think it lies at the environmental heart of the CDFMP. This is not the case for the OHL corridor. It is also apparent that the officials did not think the OHL corridor to be especially important in itself, as otherwise they would not have been content in principle with the (largely) blocking of that corridor under the revised N2. Again this appears to have been for good reason since the “corridor” did not have any particular pre-existing function apart from containing the OHL. The proposed access connections in terms of the CDFMP were no doubt useful, but not fundamental to the overall design at least where it can be assumed a new design would seek to replace or compensate these one way or another. This in turn suggests an overstatement in Mr Black’s position to the contrary. It would also appear implicit in the officers’ support for the “principle of additional dwellings” that they well understood the need for efficiency of housing development, as explained in detail by Mr John Findlay, but hardly mentioned by Mr Black.

[202] In these circumstances the hypothetical purchaser would be taking on a negotiation in an already constructive relationship with the ACC MDC team. In all probability this would have taken the form of discussions over the content for a revised CDFMP in a no-scheme world. There would have been good prospects of a mutually satisfactory design outcome for development of the OHL corridor. We think the hypothetical purchaser would need to assess, as best it could on incomplete information, where the council’s “red line” in the negotiation would be on the matter of retained open space. In this case the information would have been incomplete because there had not been a detailed design to the level of a design and access statement or a masterplan. Such a document would have illustrated and sought to justify the quantity and uses of proposed open space in a no-scheme world and address the “ripple effect” elsewhere caused by the additional housing, to which the officers could have provided a reaction. Absent this level of detailed information, we think that the hypothetical purchaser’s approach would have had to be both broad and cautious.

[203] Reading in particular the letter of 3 April 2019, the hypothetical purchaser would have noted ACC’s view that the line of the OHL “allows for valuable allotment and amenity space, which is paramount to the sustainable success of Countesswells.” It would have noted that ACC were “comfortable with the principle of additional dwellings being accommodated on (the OHL corridor) and that ACC’s “primary objective is quality placemaking, and we see that this proposal is an opportunity for betterment in development form." The letter also refers to the potential (MSC) planning application being accompanied with a design and access statement which would show how the levels of amenity space including relocation of the play space and allotments were to be delivered in suitable locations across the site. We think that the need for a design and access statement should not be underestimated. The design and access statement submitted in 2014 was a detailed document, in some respects equivalent in detail to the CDFMP. There would thus be scope for ACC’s officers to limit the amount of OHL space they would agree to be given up for housing. So we agree with Mr Black, at least up to a point, that ACC were reserving their position in respect of the balance between additional houses and lost open space. In this we also think that Mr Black had a point in that it is difficult to see how a loss of all the OHL open space could be seen as an “improvement” in placemaking. Mr Lewis would probably have wanted the retention of some “openness” beyond the play area and allotments on or around N2, in the sense of keeping a recreational area. So he and his officials might not necessarily have been satisfied that “pepper potted” open space compensated for the whole loss in planning terms.

[204] In these circumstances we think the hypothetical purchaser would have looked to where development prospects were strongest in its favour. The “central” 1.82 ha area of open space is prescribed little particular use. It is described as general open space. It is not part of any park. The only specific use it has under the CDFMP is for paths set off from streets suitable for walking, cycling and equestrian use. As Mr MacDonald put it, he had run out of things to place there in the design, and the location did not suggest a need for retaining landscaping. Mr Truscott accepted that low density houses could go there and only suggested the retention of some form of “green linkage” to remain. The masterplan shows various green linkages of various widths, throughout the development, depending upon the importance of the link. In the case of the central area, we doubt that the linkage there, running as it does along the periphery of the site, could be classed as important as other wider green linkages, such as Core Path 57. So we do not think that the hypothetical purchaser, exercising caution, would need to assume that more than say a 10m wide strip might need to be required for the approx. 285m length of the area as a green linkage; i.e. some 0.285ha (0.70 acres) of land might need to be reserved for this eventuality. On the whole, we consider that residential development would have appeared to have very good prospects of securing officer support for 1.82ha - 0.285ha = say 1.535ha (3.79 acres) for the central area.

[205] Turning to Hazleden Park (2 ha, recalculated at 1.76 ha) the informed purchaser would be aware that ACC would be likely to require the retention of the large play zone of a minimum size of 0.25ha. Mr MacDonald had suggested a larger area of 0.4ha in N13 to include a large play area, but not including allotments. We understood the required space for allotments under the CDFMP to be about 0.25 ha in size, since the CDFMP provided for two allotment areas totalling 0.5 ha. We think the conservative approach we have discussed would require to assume that these uses (totalling 0.65ha) could not be compensated out of open space elsewhere, and would require to remain at Hazleden Park or take the place of housing in the vicinity.

[206] The question is how much more compensatory open space might require to be retained in the eyes of the ACC MDC team, in addition to the 0.65 ha above. It is quite possible that the answer is none, in the light of Mr MacDonald’s evidence. But we think the hypothetical purchaser would need to look at making a generous open space “offer,” essentially one which ACC officers would find difficult not to support. As Hazleden Park is designated “local open space,” the relevant requirement is a size between 0.4 and 2 ha. In terms of quality, we felt that Mr Truscott’s comment could not be discounted, namely that without Hazleden Park the northern section of the site had relatively little open space. If not expressed as a crude position, it is implicit in both letters (e.g.“… we generally seek quality of space, clearly defined, rather than quantity which will be far more desirable than is currently proposed under an overhead line …”) that the council was prepared to trade, so to speak, quality for quantity. Very broadly, we think that a proposal which left one-half of Hazleden Park or equivalent nearby as open space, including the allotments and large play area, and the other half to additional housing and infrastructure, would have found favour with the planners. Such a proposal would, we infer, have presented as a genuine “win/win” position between developer and planners and would have been be an “offer” which the ACC officers would find difficult not to support. This would reduce the size of the park to 0.88ha – still over double the minimum required size for local open space – and would provide a certain amount of “openness” potentially sought by Mr Lewis for a recreation area. There would also be enough room for some form of green linkage towards Core Path 57. No doubt a design could be found which used the retained open space to provide landscaping to break up housing in a way which retained a rural feel. Above all, the residual open space would be of significantly higher quality than that which exists in the with-scheme world because of the removal of the OHL.

[207] The applicants only own 1.42 ha of the 1.76 ha attributed to the design of Hazleden Park. The remaining 0.34ha to the north belongs to a third party. Logic might suggest that the owner of the 0.34ha would be content to propose to ACC, alongside CDL, that the new allocation of open space in a no scheme world would be shared by landowners in equal proportion. On the face of it both would benefit in principle from removal of the OHL. However, we think the cautious purchaser would be reluctant to assume that the making of a satisfactory agreement with a third party landowner would necessarily be concluded in the future. So adopting a conservative approach we shall assume all the reallocated open space would come from the applicants’ land: i.e. 1.42 ha – 0.88 ha = 0.54 ha (1.33 acres) NDA for residential use. But we shall bear in mind the potential upside for the hypothetical purchaser in the event that an agreement could be concluded, thus potentially freeing a little more of the applicants’ land for development.

[208] Turning the hypothetical purchaser’s attention to Wardhead Park at 1.15ha, this area of local open space was intended to be less formal than Hazleden Park. It includes a play zone of unspecified size under the CDFMP, whereby the minimum size is 0.15ha. Mr MacDonald’s evidence suggests that the park is not required at all on account of its proximity to Central Park. He may be correct, but again however taking a cautious approach we cannot overly discount Mr Truscott’s evidence. He suggested that the park was worthy of its location in the context of the nearest alternative areas of open space. Without it, the C7 area in particular may lose its rural feel to some extent, and the function of breaking up adjacent housing could be compromised. There is also a small green connection potentially running towards Core Path 57 which could be lost. Bearing these points in mind, in the context of the loss of most of the central area to housing as discussed above, we feel that the hypothetical purchaser would need to retain a significant amount of open space for a park to be confident of officer’s support. As Mr Lewis indicated, the issues are similar for the southern section as they are for the northern section. As we have indicated, the adjacent (and now recalculated larger) central area would be developed mainly for housing on the hypothesis discussed above, thus making a stronger case for the retention of open space. In these circumstances we think that the hypothetical purchaser, taking a broad and cautious view, would have thought itself to have strong prospects in acquiring planning permission for housing on one half of the Wardhead Park land, and by leaving the other half for open space including a play zone, landscaping and a green corridor, say 0.575 ha (1.42 acres). This is still over the minimum requirement for local open space of 0.4ha.

[209] In reaching the above conclusions we do not think that development in the OHL corridor at this limited scale could be perceived as undermining the principles of the CDFMP. We also think that the remaining open space provided by the hypothetical purchaser would be very likely to meet any conceivable objection on behalf of SNH/NatureScot or a community council. SNH, if inclined to take a stand, would not have a strong position in objecting to any proposal for the OHL corridor simply because the land has long been farmland and does not attract any high priority wildlife interest. We would be confident that a new design would be mindful for the creation new nature corridors. We were not struck that the ES would be likely to require amendment. Mr Lewis did not think so, although we suppose the risk cannot be ignored altogether. We also think that the fairly generous retention of open space, no longer constrained by the OHL, would be likely to satisfy any objection by a community council. We bear in mind that one community council had previously regarded the OHL open space as unsatisfactory because of the presence of the OHL, so could hardly reasonably object to a smaller but more meaningful area.

[210] So to conclude we think that ACC officers would have regarded removal of the OHL as a material change of circumstances, and if not certain, it is a near certainty that they would have been minded to support or permit residential development of some sort on a proportion of the OHL open space. Taking a necessarily broad and conservative approach we consider that there would have been very good prospects of success for additional development on approximately 2.65 ha (Central 1.535 ha + Hazleden 0.54 ha + Wardhead 0.575 ha) (6.55 acres) of the open space belonging to the applicants, while leaving the remaining 1.74 ha (4.39 ha – 2.65 ha) as open space and green corridor.

[211] It follows that we reject the respondents’ approach that planning prospects were very limited, and that land value should be assessed “bottom up” on the basis of agricultural value. We think that a top down approach is appropriate, to which we now turn.

Valuation issues – applicants’ submissions

[212] The applicants’ submissions made reference to the Scott Schedule and table of comparables. It will be recalled that the total no-build zone (4.39 ha/10.85 acres) included nibs of land which would not be developed on account of design issues related to the OHL. Mr MacDonald’s design has not been criticised in the sense that he had over-mitigated by excluding development on too much land or had otherwise under-mitigated.

[213] It was right that account be taken of the planning requirement for 24.5% affordable housing in valuing the claim. The purchaser carrying out due diligence would understand that affordable housing would likely be provided by the applicant towards the centre of the site as had in fact occurred. Hitherto affordable housing had been developed at a rate above 30 dpa. Mr Court had proposed a conservative rate of 23 dpa (box 5), based on advice from CDL that they envisaged the overall density of affordable housing at 23 dpa across the development. The applicants pointed out that the passage in Arnold White Estates referring to the loss caused to the landowner by not being able to sell to other developers meant that the applicant can be considered one of the potential buyers. This added weight to the point that the applicant had set out how it would have developed the land in terms of density and site coverage.

[214] Mr Stevens’ affordable rate of 14.10 dpa equated to an 80:20 split in terms of area. This ratio had been extrapolated from Mr Loomes’ analysis of the Mains of Countesswells sale, but Mr Loomes’ notional density had been 17 dpa for low rise affordable housing, so it was incorrect for Mr Stevens to start with the 80:20 ratio to derive a lower density. Mr Stevens’ rate of 14.10 dpa was too low. It was lower than some private density so far developed, albeit mostly in the more central areas of the site. It was only slightly above the private densities assumed by Mr Stevens (11.36 dpa) and Mr Court (10.22 dpa). It was submitted that Mr Stevens’ density would not be consistent with the efficient use of land and the plots would be too big for the units being provided. Mr Court’s figure should be preferred.

[215] The next issue related to house size and site coverage (box 6) which were inter-related. Mr Stevens’ choice of 116.1 sqm (1,250 sq ft) was too small. This represented mid-market housing which would not sit well on the spacious plots which would be available. His housing density would lead to a very low coverage of 1,320 sqm per acre whereas development on the ground thus far produced a rate of 1,607 sqm per acre. Mr Court had adopted the applicants’ suggested coverage of 15,500 sq ft per acre (1,440 sqm per acre) which, when applied to the 9.49 acre private site, gave a total development of 147,095 sq ft or 13,665.1 sqm. It was from this coverage that the average footprint of 140.9sqm (1,516 sq ft) was derived for the 97 private units. This average unit size was conservative and justified, and had already been built in more central locations. Coverage should determine the average footprint, not vice versa.

[216] Turning to sales revenue (box 7) the applicants submitted that both experts used information from the sale of block N10, but Mr Stevens used the whole basket whereas Mr Court used the rate for house sizes above 100 sqm. It was submitted that Mr Court’s approach was more logical given that the OHL corridor would have provided a better quality site, particularly in the southern section.

[217] Turning to build cost (box 11) which was relevant only to the residual valuation, there was nothing to suggest that Mr Court’s approach was not justified. Referring to marketing incentives (box 16) it was submitted that to add a provision for part exchanges over and above the standard 5% incentive allowance would be significant. There was no basis for such an assumption since the applicants had been able to sell their properties within the 5% incentive.

[218] Commenting upon the comparable evidence, it was pointed out that the three smaller sales were centre of site sales, so arguably not as attractive to the market. The big Barratt 2 transaction, which post-dated the relevant date, encompassed a significant number of locations with a variety of dates of likely build out. The Mains of Countesswells acquisition was for land not to be developed for some time and contrary to the evidence of Mr Stevens, there was no discount for delayed development as indicated by Mr Loomes. The large Barratt 2 and Mains of Countesswells transactions showed land being paid for well in advance of the likely development of the land, without discount. It was submitted that the comparable evidence was more reliable, but that regard could be had to both comparable and residual approaches.

[219] The applicants disputed Mr Stevens’ approach to make a significant discount for “delayed receipt”. His approach assumed the sites would continue to be developed as they have been until the development as a whole is completed. He also assumed that the applicant would exercise their purchase options. There was no basis for such assumptions and it should be recalled that one was considering the sale at the valuation date, without any restriction as to when the land could be developed, so it was not logical to assume that a seller would sell at a heavily discounted price. It was reasonable to assume that large blocks of land could be sold off, as occurred in the Barratt 2 transaction. The respondents had no basis for taking into account land not in the ownership of the applicants. It would not be possible for the applicants to recover compensation for land affected by an OHL under option as there would be no certainty the applicants would require it. The same logic should apply to discounted receipt. The applicants’ OHL land was being effectively devalued because they happen to own a large quantity of adjacent land and had options over more, which was not a proper approach in assessing compensation. The respondents’ position fell foul of the reality principle discussed in Secretary of State for Transport v Curzon Park Limited : Lewison LJ at paragraph 42. The exercise of the options, thus expanding the applicants’ landholding, was a post-valuation date event which was not inevitable at the valuation date.

Valuation issues – respondents’ submissions

[220] The respondents submitted that we should follow Mr Stevens’ approach in land valuation. The respondents highlighted the divergence between Mr Court’s residual and comparable valuations (£12,892,000 and £10,750,000). It could be inferred something was far wrong with the inputs. The difference could not be explained simply by increasing the 20% profit margin to 25% in the residual appraisal in which, as Mr Stevens indicated, the lower percentage reflected the general market approach. It could be inferred that Mr Court’s residual valuation had been based upon unrealistic assumptions.

[221] The respondents submitted that Mr Court’s private/affordable split, by applying an affordable housing density of 23 dpa was unsound. No detailed analysis had been given as to how the figure had been arrived at. In effect such density would result in 87.47% of the land being used for private housing with only 12.53% allocated to affordable housing. This had a significant effect on the outcome of the valuation exercise and required a detailed evidential basis. On the other hand Mr Steven’s split of 80:20 private/affordable was supported by the evidence of Mains of Countesswells as provided by Mr Loomes. It was not fair for Mr Court to suggest Mr Loomes’ position had been one of “advocacy” in seeking to acquire the land as cost effectively as possible. The fact was that Mains of Countesswells had resulted in a transaction.

[222] It was submitted that Mr Stevens’ revised headline rate for private land at £1,155,631 (box 21) was firmly based on the comparable evidence. Less weight should be given to Barratt 2 which occurred after the valuation date. Nevertheless, as Mr Stevens put it, there was a compelling picture of uniformity across the site.

[223] There was no justification for Mr Court’s adding a premium of 10% to the average of the comparables. Mr Stevens had concluded there was little to support the view that the OHL site was higher quality, given that the comparable transactions themselves covered a range of sites.

[224] Counsel adopted Mr Stevens’ position which was that the benefit of any additional housing land would only accrue to the applicant in due course. The consented housing allocation at Countesswells is very large in the context of the Aberdeen market and would take years to build and sell out. Additional housing land release would not have an impact on the rate at which the applicants are able to sell or build out their existing allocation. It is only after their existing allocation has been built out or sold that the additional land release would provide the applicant with an additional receipt.

[225] Mr Stevens had calculated that as at the relevant date, the applicants had within their ownership or control, an existing unsold allocation of 2,015 units. Based on land sales on average of 120 private houses being sold each year, and allowing for a lead in time of two years, the applicants would not benefit from any additional land release for 14.5 years after the relevant date. The value of any additional development land would require to be discounted in accordance with Mr Stevens’ calculations. Although the Barratt 2 transaction had involved the potential for a very large number of units, the land being paid for in two instalments 12 months apart, Mr Stevens had pointed out that the figure of 120 units per annum was an average. The fact that Barratts had bought a larger allocation in 2020 simply meant it would be several years before they were in the market to buy more. Moreover the applicants’ claim was premised on all of the existing allocation and the OHL strip being eventually developed and sold, otherwise the applicants would have suffered no loss at all. It was submitted that Mr Stevens’ evidence on timing had not been challenged.

[226] The respondents did not accept that their position was undermined by the “reality principle”. It was possible to look at the triggering of options as a “perception of future possibility” as at the valuation date.

Discussion and conclusions on valuation issues

[227] As the case proceeded it became apparent that both parties had distanced themselves from assessing development value on a residual appraisal approach, although both Mr Court and Mr Stevens had carried out such an appraisal from an early stage. Their reasons for changing their mind were somewhat different. Mr Court departed from the residual approach when it became apparent that his figures did not sit well with his assessment based upon comparable evidence. Mr Stevens preferred the comparable evidence in the light of the compelling picture of uniformity, as he put it, which was further emphasised once details of the Mains of Countesswells transaction became known. We agree with Mr Stevens’ description of the comparable evidence. We think there is little to be added by attempting a residual appraisal which is sensitive to a large number of input assumptions.

[228] We were struck by the fact that Mr Loomes used a straightforward and simple rate per acre approach in negotiating the Mains of Countesswells transaction. He took the view that a “high level” approach was necessary because there was a lack of detail on the number and value of units which would emerge. This was also the approach of Mr Fawcus in negotiating the Barratt 2 transaction, even although more detail about units was available because the CDFMP was more developed in respect of the areas being purchased. Accordingly we think a “high level” approach is in line with the broad approach which would be taken by the hypothetical purchaser in the present case.

[229] Mr Stevens took a weighted average of the three smaller comparable transactions in the table of comparables, namely Kirkwood Homes, Barratt 1 and CHAP, resulting in a figure of £1,155,631 per NDA for private housing. He does not appear to have introduced the Mains of Countesswells transaction into his average, although the rate per acre is very similar. We think it is more appropriate to take a simple average of the four transactions, although this does not make much difference to the overall rate: £1,150,500 per NDA for private housing. We recognise it is likely that parts of the OHL site will be more valuable than others, namely the higher ground roughly between C6 and C7. We are less clear whether this will produce a higher overall average than any of the comparables, which had areas with views to woodlands and natural spaces. The experts differed on this point. We do not propose to make any express allowance for this possibility, however, on the basis that we are addressing a hope value claim and the hypothetical purchaser would be taking a conservative approach.

[230] Given that we have good comparable evidence based on a rate per acre, we do not feel it necessary to attempt to assess a rate per plot or rate per sqm coverage. To do so would introduce more assumptions and would only risk widening the range of possible values. Parties did analyse the transactions so as to include a rate per unit or plot. The analyses also provide details by which a proposed density can be calculated, which is a related issue. It can be seen that the transaction showing the highest plot value (Mains of Countesswells) has the lowest density, whereas the transaction with the lowest plot value (Barratt 1) has the highest density. This is entirely predictable in itself, but what is important is that the overall rate per acre is within a very tight range for all transactions. In other words, the evidence suggests that a detailed assessment of potential density and rates per unit is not likely to add very much to the final analysis.

[231] The above point is underlined by the fact that some of the competing density figures have given rise to difficulty. For example, parties generally agreed that overall density should be approximately 11.9 dpa, which equates to about 30 units per hectare, being the minimum density required by ACC (Scott Schedule, Appendix B , box 3). However in the context of the injurious affection claim Mr Court estimated that on an affected area of 2.922 ha or 7.22 acres, there would be 30 affordable houses on 1.22 acres of land and 94 private units on 6 acres of land. This equates to an overall density of 17.17 dpa. This is substantially in excess of, and inconsistent with, the overall density he has assumed for the first claim in box 3.

[232] There is also a difficulty with an estimate based upon average house footprint and coverage per acre. In box 6 Mr Court has taken a figure of 140.9 sqm average footprint which equates to 1,440 sq m coverage per acre. This is inconsistent with Mr Court’s diminution in value calculation which assumes coverage at 1,607 sqm per acre.

[233] We now turn to the issue of density of affordable housing. The number of houses overall will be a product of the planning authority’s minimum density requirement which parties have agreed is approximately 11.9 units per acre. The total number of houses can thus be calculated for any given area. The number of these which will be affordable is important, since affordable units are likely to be more dense on site and thus govern the amount of private land as will be available. ACC’s requirement of 24.5% affordable housing is a percentage of the total number of houses to be built, and is in a sense a roof tax. It is therefore necessary to assess the amount of land which that number of affordable houses will occupy.

[234] We think the starting point is to consider what actual type of affordable houses would be required in the no-scheme world. It is no doubt the case that many or most of the affordable houses to date have been built at the centre of the development. The density figures to date are in excess of 30 dpa, which would imply flats. Mr Court’s figure of 23 dpa is an average for the CDFMP as a whole, which reduces housing densities from the central area outwards. The OHL corridor is a relatively outward area. We think the planning authority can be assumed to wish to seek a wide range of affordable houses across the development for all needs. So we do not think it can be assumed that the authority would be content for development on the OHL to comprise much other than fairly low density family houses with gardens appropriate to the location. We are conscious that in practice CDL were able to control much of the site, so that much of the affordable housing was built at the centre of the development. But we do not think the hypothetical purchaser emerging in 2018 could safely assume the planning authority would agree to offset the requirement by permitting the affordable housing to be built in more central areas instead of the OHL corridor.

[235] Mr Loomes’ negotiated affordable density in the Mains of Countesswells transaction was 17 dpa. We understood this to comprise two-storey buildings, but not flats or apartments: in other words most likely terraced and semi-detached houses. We think this would be consistent with the type of dwelling to be required for the OHL corridor. We think it unlikely that the density for the OHL corridor would be much greater than this figure. On the other hand we feel that an affordable density of 14.10 dpa put forward by Mr Stevens is a very low density. While we understand his point that the Mains of Countesswells land would be somewhat nearer to the development centre than the OHL land, we still feel his figure would be unlikely to be provided in practice. We note that Mr Loomes did not apply a rule of thumb for an 80:20 split between private and affordable areas.
