His figure was based upon the nature of the affordable housing in question, which produced the density of 17 dpa. So for Mr Stevens to extrapolate an 80:20 split between private and affordable housing is something of a gloss upon Mr Loomes’ approach.

[236] Accordingly we think it would be fairly safe for the hypothetical purchaser to assume an affordable density of 17 dpa, which (coincidently) provides an approximate 83:17 area split with land for private housing.

[237] In these circumstances we have calculated a full development value for an overall area of 2.65 ha or 6.55 acres. We refer to our calculation at Appendix C . In summary the greenfield value (£1,150,500 on 5.44 acres private housing) requires the addition of the value of 19 affordable units (£25,000 per plot). The sum requires the deduction of the cost of section 75 agreements on all 78 units (£17,222 per unit.) The overall net land value is therefore £5,392,120 or £823,224 per acre.

[239] We now turn to the respondents’ discounting argument. It is contended that the benefit of any additional housing land would only really accrue to the applicants once they had developed the whole site. All that the provision of the OHL land would do is displace the existing phasing. As at the valuation date the development had consent for 3,090 residential units; once that was completely built out the additional units would become units 3,091 to 3,218. Only once that stage was reached, so it was argued, could it be said that the applicants had suffered a loss on account of denial of development on the OHL land.

[240] The argument perhaps finds some support in the concept that the “value to the owner” principle may in some circumstances produce less compensation than would be quantified by reference to open market value: Arnold White Estates at paragraph 28. So if the particular owner is CDL it would seem possible, at least in principle, to look at their particular circumstances; i.e. to take account of any large amount of land already held by them.

[241] However it is apparent that at the valuation date CDL did not in fact own the large areas of land at the south of the site comprising Mains of Countesswells and Colthill Farm. These were the main areas still to be developed. CDL only “controlled” these in the sense that they held purchase options, which options we understood for the most part still required to be triggered. The Mains of Countesswells option agreement has been analysed as a comparable to assist in the task of valuation, but it was not suggested that CDL owned the land at the valuation date.

[242] We were referred to Secretary of State for Transport v Curzon Park Limited . Lewison LJ amplified the reality principle at [42], by referring to his dissenting judgment in Harbinger Capital Partners v Caldwell [2013] EWCA Civ 492, pointing out that his colleagues had not disagreed with his statement of principle. He had said:-

“[22] There are many areas of law in which an amount is to be ascertained by postulating a hypothetical transaction of one kind or another … Sometimes the hypothesis is statutory and sometimes it is contractual. The courts have developed a well-established set of principles that apply to both kinds of case. The most important of these is that things are to be taken as they are in reality on the valuation date, except to the extent that the instrument postulating the hypothetical transaction requires a departure from reality. In the old cases this is summarised in the Latin phrase rebus sic stantibus . In the more modern cases it has been described as the principle of reality: Hoare v National Trust (1998) 77 P&CR 366.

[23] The following points amplify the reality principle:

(i) The hypothesis is only a mechanism for enabling one to arrive at a value of particular property for a particular purpose. It does not entitle the valuer to depart from the real world further than the hypothesis compels: Hoare v National Trust , 380 (Schiemann LJ). The various hypotheses must be taken no further than their terms make strictly necessary: Cornwall Coast County Club v Cardgrange Limited [1987] 1 EGLR 146, 152. It is necessary to adhere to reality subject only to giving full effect to the hypothesis: Hoare v National Trust , 387 (Peter Gibson LJ).

(ii) Giving effect to the hypothesis may require a legal impediment to the implementation of the hypothesis to be ignored or treated as overridden; but only to the extent necessary to enable the hypothesis to be effective: IRC v Crossman [1937] AC 26; The Law Land Company Ltd v Consumers Association Ltd [1980] 2 EGLR 109; Walton v IRC [1996] STC 98.

(iii) The world of make believe should be kept as near as possible to reality: Trocette Property Co Ltd v GLC (1972) 28 P & CR 408, 420 (Lawton LJ); Hoare v National Trust , 386 (Peter Gibson LJ). Reality must be adhered to so far as possible: Cornwall Coast County Club v Cardgrange Ltd, 150 (Scott J). The valuer should depart from reality only when the hypothesis so requires: Hoare v National Trust 388 (Peter Gibson LJ).

(iv) Where the hypothesis inevitably entails a particular consequence, the valuer must take that consequence into account: East End Dwellings Co Ltd v Finsbury BC [1952] AC 109, 132.

(v) But there is a clear distinction between hypotheses expressly directed to be made and assumptions allegedly consequential on the express hypotheses. Where the alleged consequence is not inevitable, but merely possible (or even probable), then the consequence cannot be assumed to have happened: Cornwall Coast County Club v Cardgrange Ltd 149 (Scott LJ).

(vi) The reality principle applies at the valuation date. Events which post-date the valuation date cannot generally be taken into account. But the purchaser will have regard to future possibilities, and it is a perception of future possibilities that matters. There is, in this respect, a clear difference between events before and after the valuation date. What has happened before the valuation date is either known (because it really happened) or is required by the hypothesis to be assumed to have happened. But the future is unknowable. Assumptions about the future should not be made. Nor can a Tribunal make findings of fact about the future. So all that a purchaser (and by extension a valuer) can do is assess the effects on current value of future possibilities.”

[243] In the present case, it was not inevitable as at the valuation date that the various purchase options would have been exercised in the future. The fact that CDL might do so in a with-scheme world would no doubt have appeared likely, since the options had been negotiated and formalised and the development was proving to be a success, but it could not be described as an inevitable course. The options still had to be triggered. In these circumstances the applicants found upon paragraph [23](v) of Lewison LJ’s principles, whereas the respondents found upon sub-paragraph (vi) in the sense that the position as at the valuation date could be regarded as a perception of future possibilities.

[244] It seems to us that the present situation is closer to paragraph (v). The valuation hypothesis in issue here is the above mentioned “value to owner” principle. CDL were owners of the OHL land and held the options. The fact that the options would likely have been triggered is merely an assumption allegedly consequential upon CDL holding those options. As the consequence was not inevitable, it cannot be assumed to have happened. On this part of the reality principle the respondents’ argument for discounting loss would fall to be rejected.

[245] We think the analysis can be carried further. In present context we think the value to owner principle and the reality principle are two sides to the same coin. One has to look to see whether these applicants have sustained a loss, and to do that one should look to the reality of the situation as far as possible. One also has to bear in mind other familiar principles such as duty to mitigate. Looking at the matter this way, the respondents imply that in order to minimise a loss, the applicants are first required to exercise the options by acquiring all the optioned land for development. We are uneasy about this as a proposition, since for aught yet seen that may or may not be a reasonable commercial position to adopt in the future, and one which at the relevant date could not have appeared to be risk free because future economics are involved. Moreover it is highly questionable why CDL, if a hypothetical transacting party, should notionally have to choose between developing the OHL land which they already own, and the optioned land which they would have to pay for. This situation seems to be a departure from reality too far. The reality is CDL have lost the use of their own OHL land. So we do not think that the fact they “controlled” much of the larger site calls for a discount for the amount of time it takes to develop the land which they do not yet own or indeed may never own.

[246] It was not suggested that there should be any other form of discounting on account of timing issues under this head, although there was such an argument for the injurious affection claim. In essence Mr Stevens had contended that losses for the northern corridor should be discounted for two years and for the southern corridor for five years on account of the time it would take to achieve sales at those locations. We shall deal with the point here.

[247] While there is a certain logic to Mr Stevens’ position, and we have accepted similar arguments in other cases, we do not feel it is borne out by the comparable evidence drawn to our attention in this case. Mr Stevens did not produce convincing market evidence of discounting. For example, the headline price for Mains of Countesswells was discounted by 10% to reflect certain planning risks, but Mr Loomes’ evidence before us did not appear to suggest a specific discount for timing. The background was that CDL had expected the land to be traded out in three to five years. So Mr Stevens’ view that the 10% reduction was due to timing is therefore something of a gloss on Mr Loomes’ approach. It is also difficult to ignore the Barratt 2 transaction. Although this falls after the relevant date the analysis is consistent with the rate per acre achieved in the four transactions occurring prior to the relevant date, including Mains of Countesswells. We think it can probably be regarded as part of a pattern for that reason. What Barratt 2 illustrates, at least in terms of Mr Fawcus’ evidence, is that there was no discounting for timing in a transaction whereby the purchaser bought perhaps seven or eight years’ worth of its land supply, paid for within a period of about one year. This shows the considerable strength of the market in which one major developer would seek to buy a very large area of land from another such developer, and thus participate in a prestigious development for years to come. In these perhaps unusual circumstances we do not think it reasonable that development value should be reduced for the timing of sales within the sort of 2-5 year periods envisaged by Mr Stevens.

[248] There was no argument for discounting in light of the fact that the necessary wayleaves were granted for a finite period of 50 years.

Planning / hope value revisited

[249] As indicated above we think planning officers would have been perceived as likely to support a future development on approximately 2.65 ha (6.55) acres) of the OHL corridor, thus retaining approximately 1.74 ha for open space. In addition, the relatively generous densities implied in the above valuation analysis would allow for additional open space by means of “pepper potting” discussed by Mr MacDonald. We think that with the MDC team on side, prospects of securing an actual permission – most likely ultimately in the form of an MSC consent – would also have appeared very good. Nevertheless the hypothetical purchaser would require to consider the fact that a successful detailed design exercise would be required, followed by a planning process not just in the form of an MSC consent but probably also in the form of a formal amendment to the CDFMP as SG. As in the case of the 2017 addendum, there would probably have required to be public consultation and a decision by the full council, ultimately requiring ratification by Scottish Ministers. This process could not be perceived to be risk free and would take time to complete.

[250] The applicants contended that any discounting for risks from full development value to hope value should be limited and referred to the Mains of Countesswells transaction. There, the 10% discount from headline price was said to be on the basis of a very similar situation, because there was PPiP in both cases. While we accept the point about PPiP, we think the planning position is rather different for the present case. In Mains of Countesswells, the development area was broadly outlined in zones in the CDFMP, and each zone was given an indicative number of units (pp132-133). What was still required was more detailed masterplanning for those zones, and it was here perhaps there was some perceived risk of loss of unit numbers from the indicative schedule. However, in the present case a new development area along the OHL corridor would have required, in practical terms, the agreement of ACC to amend the CDFMP to alter and enlarge the development blocks, as well as to increase the specified numbers of dwellings. Otherwise, the development would require to be justified as contrary to the development plan. As we have said, the removal of the OHL would have been regarded as a material change in circumstances, and by retaining generous amounts of open space the applicants would have had very good prospects of obtaining an approval. But the difference is the residential development on the Mains of Countesswells section was already indicatively programmed in the CDFMP, which was not the case for the OHL corridor. So we think the risks would have been perceived differently.

[251] In assessing hope value we cannot improve upon the passage in a standard textbook quoted by Lord Collins in Spirerose at paragraph 72:

“A valuation to determine hope value is often impossible other than by adopting an instinctive approach, particularly in the stages when the hope of permission is remote; it can only be a guestimate of the money a speculator would be prepared to pay. As the hope crystallises into reasonable certainty of a permission at some stage, a valuation can be attempted based on the potential development value deferred for the anticipated period until permission will be forthcoming, but with some end deduction to reflect the lack of certainty. Indeed, since most developers will buy only when permission is certain (preferring an option to buy or a contract conditional on the grant of permission before certainty has been reached) any sale in the period of uncertainty will probably require a significant discount on what might otherwise appear to be the full hope value”.

[252] As we said in Strang-Steel at [142], it would be wrong to approach the matter on the basis that, because the market might not in fact be prepared to purchase other than by way of conditional agreement, the subjects must be taken to have no value where the constraints of the legislation make it impossible to use such a conditional arrangement. We must simply attempt to identify the value which would be paid in the open market if a conditional arrangement was not possible.

[253] As appears from Spirerose paragraphs [72] and [73], and the first instance report, the Tribunal had assessed hope value at £400,000 where the value with assumed planning permission was £608,000 and the existing use value was £227,500. In broad terms, the Tribunal had accepted there was a very good prospect indeed of getting planning permission for some form of redevelopment, and a good chance of getting permission for the scheme underlying the higher value. The Tribunal concluded that a purchaser would have been prepared to pay substantially more than existing use value but much less than full development value, say £400,000.

[254] In the present case there is no real “existing use” value. The open space no longer has agricultural use. On the hypothesis it is surplus open space, it cannot realistically be ascribed any value. Practice varies, but we note that in CDL’s acquisition of Bellfield Farm, payment was only made for net developable acreage and no payment was made for public open space. So here the hypothetical purchaser has no existing use to fall back upon in the event of an unfavourable planning outcome. But it would be encouraged by the fact that any issue with the planning authority would come to a question of numbers; in other words a reduced scale of development to its proposal would always have a better chance of success. Equally the hypothetical purchaser would be aware of a potential upside. By privately assuming in his price the fairly generous amount of open space we have discussed, there would be remain an opportunity to negotiate for more housing with ACC. Such an opportunity is implicit in Mr MacDonald’s position. We have also taken a fairly conservative estimate of development value by erring on the side of caution. But there will always come a point when any purchaser will perceive paying a particular price in the face of uncertainty runs a risk too far. This factor cannot be underestimated. So in these circumstances, inevitably approaching the matter very broadly, we think a discount of somewhere between one half and one third from full development value of the 6.55 acres, say 40%, is appropriate to reach an assessment of hope value. That would reduce the £5,392,120 to £3,235,272, i.e. a hope value of say £3,235,000.

[255] It is necessary to stand back and look to consider whether this conclusion is reasonable. £3.24m is the equivalent of the full development value of about 3.93 acres, just larger than the size of the central area (less a green corridor) at 3.79 acres, in effect conceded by Mr Truscott as having potential for low density housing. Or it is about 36% of the full development value of the whole 10.85 acres of the OHL corridor. A discount of 40% to reach hope value is a substantial discount for the areas where there are very good prospects of planning permission, but equally on the evidence we have not discounted for the timing issues. So we think our assessment is reasonable.

Injurious affection claim

Applicants’ submissions

[256] The applicants submitted that there were visual amenity and potential health and safety implications of living within 45m of a pylon or an OHL. It was not surprising that Mr Stevens, until he changed his mind, and Mr Court both concluded that the sale of units in such a location would be affected. Mr Shearer had agreed with “the basic argument in certain cases.”

[257] Counsel drew attention to the fact that Mr Stevens had changed his position solely on the basis of Mr MacLeod’s written statement. Mr MacLeod had only referred to transactions at Hazelwood and Grandhome. But it was clear at the time of the relevant reports that there were no sales of any units within 45m of an OHL at Hazelwood and there was no concluded sale at Grandhome of relevance. Mr MacLeod had accepted that Dandara had considered undergrounding the relevant line at Hazelwood which would, amongst other things, have prevented reduction in value of houses close to the line. The line having not been undergrounded, and no houses having been built within 45m, itself indicated that building residential accommodation so close to a line is problematic. Counsel drew attention to Mr MacLeod’s witness statement that “houses are usually at a sufficient distance as to not make a difference in their value” which tended to support the applicants’ claim.

[258] Counsel submitted that Mr Shearer’s evidence was unreliable and his report stating that homes at Hazlewood only 45m from the OHL sold for the same price as homes over 190m from the OHL was seriously misleading. It was difficult to pass this off as a simple error since if he had measured the distance to the closest house now built (plot 35) as he claimed, he could not have allowed his report, referring to “ homes ” to stand. Nor had Mr Shearer given correct details of the Grandhome site, i.e. not that Dandara’s offer was not the highest, but that the latter had decided not to complete the sale. Mr Shearer had not investigated the planning position which would have disclosed that Dandara had considered undergrounding the Hazelwood OHL.

[259] The new material introduced on the Hazelwood development concerning plots 33, 34 and 35 added nothing. It would in any event be materially unfair to draw conclusions from it given the basis on which it was admitted, without the opportunity for the applicants’ witnesses being able to comment. The material was infected by the manifest inadequacies of Mr Shearer’s evidence. Emails relevant to the transaction were not disclosed by Mr Shearer when he gave evidence, despite having been available. Given the shortcomings of the evidence of Mr MacLeod and Mr Shearer, it was surprising that Mr Stevens had changed his mind to find that there was no diminution in value on account of the OHL.

[260] Counsel drew attention to the email by Ms Malek whereby a 15% discount was applied to the appraisal of new dwellings close to an OHL, and alluded to plots closest to the power lines being harder to sell. She made a reference to prices having increased dramatically for the last plots, but that was a reference to a rising market and not to the absence of a diminution in value on account of the OHL. Although her email is unclear as to the stand-off zone, the fact was that houses simply could not have been built within 20m of the pylon line, so her position could be equated with a 25m outer zone as taken in the present case.

[261] Counsel also referred to the evidence of Mr Fawcus in which CDL considered that the OHL would have a negative impact on the value of dwellings in close proximity to it, and that this view was shared by the director of Barratt Homes who had initially asked to purchase land away from the OHL.

[262] The applicants also referred to the Sims and Dent report. There was no reason to ignore it on account of age and it had been relied upon by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland in McKibben in 2018. It may have involved a larger line and pylons but there was also a large no-build zone ranging 40-70m in width. The study also gave a valuable insight into perceptions by valuers and agents which suggested that the OHL indeed diminished value.

[263] Counsel also pointed out that the Dandara evidence supported a diminution in value given their attempt to underground the line at Hazelwood and that no houses were built within 45m of the line.

[264] The dispute as to the extent of the affected areas within a 25m outer zone had been narrowed, and the applicants were content to use Mr Stevens’ fresh analysis of areas originally provided by OPEN. As regards Mr Stevens’ further commentary, the private/affordable split at 80:20 was disputed for reasons already given. Secondly, it would be wrong to exclude developable road corridors. This had been justified in Mr Court’s coverage of 1,607 sq m per acre which would include roads, since his average density taken from existing plots had included roads. Mr Court’s broad brush approach was appropriate where the form of development was unknown. Thirdly, the mixed use plots of N13 should be included since there would likely be residential use in upper floor apartments. It was not accepted that the value of commercial development would not be influenced by the presence of the OHL. Reference was made to the Prime Four Business Park nearby which had undergrounded the OHL. It would be wrong to assume a 100% certainty that there would be no discount at all at N13.

[265] The applicants supported Mr Court’s broad approach for diminution in value, i.e. 10% of sales overall; it was artificial to try to assess the impact by reference to a masterplan layout; and an impact at only 5% for the OHLs and 10% for the pylons was in any event too low.

[266] To the extent that Mr Stevens relied on the ASH report, counsel pointed out that the assessment in the report is very conservative, if not flawed. It was unduly restrictive by assessing impact on front rooms only and not gardens or outdoor space which was contrary to the Landscape Institute guidance, which was designed for the present type of case. The report did not reflect upon the reality of new purchasers inspecting the property and being faced for the first time with an OHL and/or pylon within 45m of their prospective plot. Mitigation planting would come too late.

[267] The applicants further submitted that Mr Truscott had under-estimated impacts in that he never found a high sensitivity to the OHL/pylons, and only very few medium-high magnitude impacts. The scale drawings by OPEN graphically illustrate the real scale of the issues.

[268] Finally, as to whether affordable housing would be affected, it was submitted that Mr Court’s approach of applying a similar percentage discount to a lower figure was more appropriate. Mr Stevens assumed a transfer of a built affordable housing unit, whereas in fact there would be a transfer of land with a design and built contract. If the latter view were taken to an extreme, e.g. if the affordable housing were constructed next to a sewage farm there would be still be no diminution in value. Mr Stevens’ discounting approach was also criticised.

Respondents’ submissions

[269] The respondents criticised Mr Court’s valuation evidence. There was very little reasoning in support of his £2.7m claim. Mr Court had used a 25m corridor but no explanation was given why a previous 10m outer corridor had been departed from. The very significant disparity between Mr Court’s and Mr Stevens’ figures indicated there was some error in approach.

[270] There had been a narrowing of the issues as to the extent of the relevant area covered by the 25m outer corridor. Distributor roads should not however be treated as part of the net developable housing land areas, which appeared to be the reason for part of the difference in respectively calculated areas. Mr Stevens had reviewed his position regarding area N13 but Mr Court had not expressly considered N13 issues.

[271] It was submitted that Mr Court had no sound basis for his methodology. His methodology was simplistic whereas Mr Stevens’ approach had carried out a sensitised residual appraisal based on a more considered reduction in house values.

[272] The respondents identified that Mr Court had assumed different densities as between the first and second claims; i.e. 11.8 dpa as opposed to17.17 dpa. It followed there was inconsistency in approach between his estimate of coverage between the two claims. Similarly there were inconsistencies in the ratio of affordable to private land between the two claims. Mr Court’s assumptions should also be treated with caution since these had been provided by CDL who had an interest in the outcome of the proceedings.

[273] The respondents accepted that the preferable approach to valuation would be to analyse sales from the plots adjacent to the OHL. This was also the view of Mr Court. There was no evidence of actual sales at the relevant date. Any reduction in sales value would be plot specific and involve the siting of each house, use of mitigation techniques and strength of the market in a specific location. Mr Stevens’ sensitised approach would be more appropriate than Mr Court’s broad approach. Mr Court’s application of a 10% reduction in value to the whole of the affected area was an over-statement of any possible loss due to injurious affection.

[274] Turning to the Sims and Dent paper, Mr Court had only referred to this in detail in evidence-in-chief, although had cited it in his rebuttal report. Mr Court had not realised that the pylons in the study were much larger than those in the present case. He had not given analysis to a finding that house prices in America could increase if the house backed on to open space under an OHL. The findings generally linked negative impacts to homes with a direct front view of pylons. Moreover Mr Court had been unable to give any reasoned evidence as to why a 10% diminution figure was accepted, which in any event did not take account of mitigation.

[275] Mr Stevens’ approach should be preferred. He was aware that the Sims and Dent study was dealing with a 275 kV OHL not a 132 kV OHL. The study did not purport to be representative of impact on housing prices on all sites in proximity to transmission lines.

[276] Mr Stevens had also taken into account the likely timing of the loss, which was the correct approach.

[277] The respondents endorsed Mr Stevens’ position which was that there would be no diminution in value for sales of affordable units. The proximity of units to the OHL would have little or no bearing to the rent driven cash flow used to calculate the existing use value for social housing.

[278] The respondents had consistently addressed the issue of effective mitigation in their evidence, particularly the ASH reports. It was pointed out that Mr Truscott had considered Mr MacDonald had over-stated the position when indicating there would be significant impacts on the visual amenity for the prospective residents. Mr MacDonald had not specifically been dealing with a 25m outer corridor and the applicants had not produced a formal VIA. Mr MacDonald had implicitly accepted that successful mitigation had been achieved.

[279] Counsel emphasised that Mr Truscott had explained why it was not appropriate to use the RVAA guidance. This guidance was of greater relevance to more over bearing structures such as wind turbines.

[280] Mr Truscott had explained why the OPEN montage had not undermined his evidence, namely that it could be seen from the orientation of buildings and screen planting that views would in fact be mitigated, and would not appear as shown by the montage. Mr Truscott had also given consideration to the existing baseline which involved the presence of three OHLs. This would reduce the sensitivity of people visiting the site as the area is known to have existing transmission lines. His position was supported by reference to the Macaulay Grange development which showed that high value houses could be built close to an OHL without deterring housebuilders. The ASH conclusions were adopted to the effect that there were likely to be few negative effects on visual amenity and that mitigation techniques had been successfully employed.

[281] The respondents described Mr Shearer’s mismatch involving the Dandara sales information to have been an oversight for which he apologised. However, he had investigated plots 33, 34 and 35 and found there to be no differential in sales value between plot 35 which was within 45m from the OHL centre line compared to the same house type 190m away.

[282] The respondents also pointed out that the Grandhome Dandara example was persuasive market evidence relating to a more prominent 275 kV OHL in close proximity to new build houses. There was no good reason why Mr Court had not carried out similar investigations. Despite Mr Fawcus’ mentioning a conversation with a Barratt director, the 2020 Barratt transaction had not resulted in any sales evidence to support a reduction in sales value. It could be implied that the purchase price agreed for the development blocks adjacent to the OHL did not disclose a discount.

[283] In context, Mr Stevens had not produced a u-turn in his evidence. He had carried out further reflection on the matter which had always been on balance.

Injurious affection – discussion and conclusion

[284] The claim has been presented on the basis that there is a diminution in value for dwellings to be built within the 25m outer corridor. Although respondents’ counsel criticised the selection of this size of corridor, we note that Mr Stevens was content to adopt it in his initial assessment whereby he accepted a diminution in value. The 25m width was selected because it approximately relates to the average depth of a plot. So in principle no claim is made for dwellings other than, as it were, the first row of plots facing the OHL. The claim is made for those dwellings which will mainly be present in the row first adjacent to the OHL. We think this is a logical approach.

[285] The ASH study has been helpful in the sense that it illustrates how views could be affected within houses in a defined area of the development. We think it was reasonable for ASH to consider a design currently specified in the CDFMP, albeit that the design specified is not conclusive and will require further refinement at the MSC stage. On the other hand we feel that the adopted threshold of “significant impact” in the context of relevant LVIA guidelines is more contentious. The guidelines are commonly used for various forms of planning appraisal. Our impression is that ASH’s approach has consequently derived from something of a public law perspective. In this area of practice, the relevance of a proposed development reducing the value of an adjacent property is something of anathema. So we did not think the study was designed essentially to determine the impact on value of a house due to adjacency to some uncongenial structure. ASH state for example “… and equally newcomers will also accept (the OHL) as they will have known nothing else when they move in …” If this is to suggest that the buyer is not likely to consider reducing his price on account of the line because he is new to the area, we disagree. We do not think the ASH results necessarily coincide with the first impression of a potential buyer visiting the site. For example by not considering impact from gardens, and by attributing less impact for rear windows, the report took a narrower approach than one might expect from a buyer’s perspective. Also of significance, the study did not address impact by looking at the setting of the individual dwellings in relation to the OHL from say the access or other external viewpoints. We think the setting would likely be an important impression in the mind of the buyer.

[286] The OPEN montages show a view of the pylons and OHL from distances of 25m, 50m and further. Speaking for ourselves, we do not think the impact on view in either scenario can be said to be insignificant. Nevertheless this was Mr Truscott’s opinion who drew attention to the fact that views from these distances would be limited on account of buildings, or in the case of a rear garden, by a screen or double screen of newly planted semi-mature trees. While we recognise there would be some screening in some cases, we are not persuaded that the impact of the OHL and pylon would be negated, particularly in winter in the likely event that the newly planted trees were deciduous.

[287] We think that the Sims and Dent study of 2004 remains an impressive piece of work despite passage of time. It contains analysis of several hundred transactions of houses built in the mid-1990s. The properties are described as mid-range, and were in the vicinity of an OHL. The study indicates that the OHL had a significant impact on selling price; within certain distances the impact of the OHL was on average 11.5% of value and, in the case of the pylons themselves the impact was up to 20.7% of value. The study does not however suggest that the figures would have general application elsewhere. The study area is part of Cumbernauld and we agree that modern design and mitigation are likely to be different in the present case. And as has been pointed out the study concerned a larger 275 kV OHL.

[288] We have some difficulty in interpreting the finding of one Sims and Dent model. Where there was a “right of way” pertaining to a house over the OHL corridor, whose rear window faced the OHL, there was an increase in value. This value increased the further away the property might be from the OHL. This finding referring only to rear views is somewhat unexplained and counter-intuitive, but it can perhaps be interpreted more generally that the use of a green OHL corridor is itself a valuable form of mitigation.

[289] Turning to Aberdeen, the written evidence of Ms Malek is unfortunately vague on detail. We feel we would need more detailed information in order to be satisfied that the site to which she refers evidences a 15% discount in sales value appraisal on account of an OHL. However, we do give some weight to her view as a sales director that “… this (health risk perception) makes the plots closest to the power lines harder to sell which generally means they are discounted in order to get them sold”. We note the comment in Sims and Dent that a review of the relevant literature indicates that the opinions of valuers and agents appear to produce a fairly reliable and accurate assessment of market value.

[290] We were struck by the fact that Mr Stevens did initially think that there would likely be a diminution in value on account of the OHL. He described his view as subconscious bias, but we think it could equally be described as an intuitive view. He changed his mind on account of “compelling” testimony from Mr MacLeod’s written statement, which is in turn related to Mr Shearer’s evidence.

[291] Having heard the foregoing evidence for ourselves, and subjected to cross-examination, we did not find it compelling. We are forced to agree with the applicants’ position that Mr Shearer’s October 2019 report stating “I am also aware that homes at Hazelwood only 45m from the OHL sell for the same price as homes over 190m from the OHL” was misleading. At the time of this report there was no completed home at Hazelwood within 45m of the OHL. If he did roughly measure the distance for a nearer marked out plot (plot 35), and thus had distances in mind, we cannot understand why he failed to notice that his report would be incorrect for the properties being expressly mentioned. Only subsequently was one dwelling (plot 35) completed within the 45m and sold. Nor did Mr MacLeod volunteer the fact that Dandara had investigated undergrounding the OHL at Hazelwood, the only conceivable purpose for which could be to improve the development potential of its land by removing the negative impact of the OHL. Nor was this matter ascertained by Mr Shearer. These facts had to be painstakingly drawn from the two witnesses in cross-examination.

[292] The respondents’ consequent salvage operation for Mr Shearer in the form of an “updated” plan and relative new information produced one Rowan type house – namely plot no. 35 – within 45m of the OHL. It sold for the same value as an apparently similar property a short distance away with less or no view of the OHL. But quite apart from the applicants’ inability to comment upon this evidence – their witnesses had already given evidence when the information was lodged – it is apparent that the prices achieved for Rowan type houses has significantly varied. For example, the evidence shows a 10% difference in price between plots 28 and 29 which could not be explained by Mr Shearer. So we do not think the Hazelwood evidence, such as it is, is robust enough to give weight to a proposition that there is no diminution in value there on account of the OHL.

[293] This position reduces the weight we can give to the Grandhome evidence. We were told that the Hazelwood experience had affected Dandara’s bid for the Grandhome site, which in any event had not resulted in a transaction. On the other hand we feel we should give some weight to the fact that Dandara had looked into undergrounding the line at Hazelwood which is a practice more generally mentioned in Ms Malek’s evidence. We also give some weight to the fact that Barratt had initially sought to avoid being required to purchase the pylon land at Countesswells.

[294] The OHL and pylons appear quite imposing. Unlike the Dandara sites, they bisect the development. In these circumstances we think it probable that there will be a diminution in selling prices at Countesswells on account of the OHL. However we think that if there were a discount to price of about 10% as suggested by Mr Court, there would have been some sales evidence to support it. There is no such evidence which we can accept, despite the presence of OHLs in housing developments being a fairly common occurance. We think it is more likely that diminution in value is effectively hidden within the 5% discount practice (and perhaps more) as is budgeted for by housebuilders. These discounts are given by a range of practices such as LBTT payments, assistance with part exchanges, provision of furnishings etc. which do not show up in the land register. This is consistent with Ms Malek’s written evidence. In assessing what that discount should be, we agree with Mr Stevens’ initial differential approach, whereby he assessed the impact was greater for properties in close proximity to a pylon than for properties only with a view of the OHL. This difference is evidenced by Sims and Dent.

[295] Absent direct sales evidence, we can only fall back upon intuition and experience: Northern Ireland Energy Networks Limited v Brickkiln Waste Limited at [29]. We find that the final assessment is very much a matter of impression. Taking into account the likelihood of good design and mitigation, we are left with the impression that there would still be a discount on first sales of about 5% for houses within 45m of a pylon and 2½% for houses within the 25m wide outer OHL corridor (i.e. lying 20-45m from the centre line of the OHL). We are fortified in this by the correlation found by Sims and Dent between valuers’ opinions and sales evidence of impact on house prices.

[296] This impact has to be calculated. Fortunately after a meeting between Mr MacDonald and Mr Stevens, parties were able to agree, subject to certain specific issues, that the housing blocks within the 25m outer corridor extended to 2.2052 ha or 5.4492 acres, (or at least to within a de minimis tolerance of that figure.) An apportionment between areas within 25m of a pylon and areas only within 25m of the OHL corridor was also agreed.

[297] As we have indicated, there was disagreement as to whether there would be any diminution in value in respect of those areas which would be required for affordable housing. Neither party has produced direct evidence from a RSL vouch the fact whether the plot acquisition price would be reduced on account of proximity to the OHL. Intuitively we would have thought it is unlikely that there would be much or any diminution in value. The affordable plot value is estimated at £25,000, which is less than one-third of the private plot value. Since it is so much less than the private value, it is difficult to see why there should be a price reduction based on normal market principles. We are not persuaded by Mr Court’s evidence to this effect.

[298] The next issue concerns block N13, part of which is a mixed use block according to the CDFMP. Mr Stevens agreed in his supplementary report that the mixed area extends to 0.6237 acres. We were advised that there would be commercial uses on the ground floor – presumably retail – and flats above. We have heard almost no evidence to the effect that commercial property is likely to sustain a diminution in value on account of an adjacent OHL. It is true that the OHL has been undergrounded at a prestigious business park nearby, but we are not persuaded that such evidence can be compared to the kind of local commercial uses in question here. We are persuaded that Mr Stevens’ fall-back approach is fairest. This is to take one half of the relevant N13 area into the calculation (0.3118 acres).

[299] There was also an issue as to whether road areas should be included in the injuriously affected areas. We understood that Mr Stevens had excluded all distributor type roads between the blocks. On the other hand the applicants calculated an area of 0.4644ha for roads, and we were advised that Mr Court had taken this figure into account in his coverage figure. If this is the case, we disagree with Mr Court’s approach. Our understanding is that Mr MacDonald had calculated the areas in the table associated with the N2 brief which had excluded roads adjoining the blocks: paragraph 2.3.8.7 of OPEN’s November 2019 report. This is the approach for the main claim. So on that basis we do not think Mr Court should have included roads for the injurious affection claim. We think that Mr Stevens’ approach is closer to a conventional calculation based on net developable acres.

[300] Turning to the methodology, we prefer Mr Stevens’ approach of using a residual valuation calculation to assess the impact upon the applicants’ development land. This translates a loss of future sales revenue into a diminution in development land value. His figures show that a 10% deduction from house sales resulted in a loss of land value of £280,000 per acre, and a 5% deduction led to a loss of land value at £140,000 per acre. Mr Court’s rough and ready approach, no doubt seeking to do the same thing, was not very transparent. His calculation (paragraph 12.10 of JB7) impliedly reduces a loss equating to 10% of revenue by 5% for incentives and, we were told, by a further 20%, in name of developer’s profit. The implication is that 75% of house sales value equates to land value. This does not sit easily with Mr Court’s comment elsewhere (CDL 40 paragraph 9.15) that a plot value representing 25.75% of revenue would be accepted by most valuers as within accepted parameters for this sort of site. Another calculation which suggests a 10% reduction in revenue from the social landlord would result in a fall in site value from £25,000 to £18,000 per unit, is unfathomable.

[301] In these circumstances we feel that Mr Stevens’ more detailed residual approach is safer. As a mathematical exercise it was not seriously challenged. Mr Steven’s residual model has also produced a land value markedly similar to the result of our comparative approach, which in turn involved some inputs agreed in the Scott Schedule, our adopted affordable densities and rate per acre of £1,150,000. Our crude checks tend to support his conclusion that a 5% reduction in sales broadly equates to a loss in land value of £140,000 per acre, and also that a 2.5% reduction in sales has a linear effect; i.e. would cause a reduction in land value of about £70,000 per acre.

[302] Finally there is the question of discounting for the fact that as at the valuation date the reduced sales would only arise in the future; in two years for the northern corridor and five years for the southern corridor. As we have indicated in our reasoning in the main claim, we might have been attracted to this point in other cases. But in the light of the comparable evidence we do not feel that a discount is justified.
